editorials.title: Deadly span: On vulture safety in India, threat of electrocution
editorials.passage:
Whereas for many decades the chief concern about vulture safety was centered on chemical threats, the threat of electrocution posed by India’s expanding power infrastructure may supersede it. In the 1990s, India’s vultures suffered one of the world’s worst population crashes, nosediving 99.5% by 2007 from a high of around four crore in the 1980s; the white-rumped, Indian, and slender-billed vultures were nearly wiped out. The culprit was diclofenac, a painkiller for cattle that wrecks vulture kidneys. The government banned the use of diclofenac , with additional bans in 2023 to mitigate threats posed by aceclofenac and ketoprofen, among some other NSAIDs. The birds’ decline left carcasses exposed for longer, supporting feral dog populations and leading to rabies outbreaks; a 2024 study in American Economic Review estimated that human mortality thus rose 4% and the associated damages cost India $69.4 billion a year. While electrocution has not become as deadly as NSAIDs have been, the fragility of the vulture population and the proliferation of unsafe power infrastructure warrant early action. One official survey reported in 2025 that vultures were nesting at only 50% of their historic nesting sites. It is no trivial detail that the raptors’ wide wingspans mean a large individual can contact two conductors at once. They also have a habit of perching on elevated structures, are attracted to open landscapes, and have incentives to congregate where the availability of food is predictable, a risk enhanced by people dumping food waste around electrical installations.

As The Hindu reported based on a recent study in the Journal of Threatened Taxa, “relocating a livestock carcass dump 2.4 km away from high-tension power infrastructure near Uttarakhand’s Dehradun may have saved these large scavengers from … electrocution”. An assessment prepared for the State Climate Resilient Power System Development Project also noted an Egyptian vulture and some steppe eagles had been electrocuted on medium-voltage, rather than high-voltage, lines. Research has noted that persistent mortality due to electrocution alone could render a local population extinct. Avian electrocution is also likely under-documented in India since dead birds can be removed by humans or scavenged. As the study indicated, one inexpensive solution is to separate vulture feeding sites from power infrastructure. Other measures to protect raptors, and even other birds, especially near settlements, include insulating conductors, increasing the gap between energised and grounded components or otherwise preventing a bird from bridging them — non-trivial considering vulture wingspans — and installing safe perches.

editorials.title: Step up regulation: On AYUSH medical education
editorials.passage:
Non-government institutions accounted for 86% of Ayurveda and 85% of homoeopathy colleges in 2024, according to government data, showing that the private sector is leading the AYUSH medical education infrastructure’s rapid expansion. Permitted seats also rose by 43% and total admission capacity by 25% between 2021 and 2024, when the Centre’s AYURGYAN allocation for AYUSH education, training, research, innovation and capacity-building, increased nearly sixfold. While similar concerns vis-à-vis allopathic medical education have been confined to whether institutions adequately prepare students for evidence-based practice, the questions of the AYUSH systems are about the quality of training and what students are being trained to practise. Given the combination, it is notable that quality issues in India’s AYUSH system long predate the current boom. In a 2005 audit, the Comptroller and Auditor General found insufficient hospital beds, outpatient services, and/or staff widespread among homoeopathy colleges, with bed occupancy from 1% to 71%. A 2020 Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine article similarly reported that many institutions had a shortfall exceeding 50% in the teaching staff required by standards then. The regulator, the National Commission for Indian System of Medicine (NCISM), has often withheld or denied permission to institutions after inspections have found gaps in faculty strength and infrastructure.

While this shows a working regulatory system, the expansion led by the private sector is of additional concern as it is accompanied by incentives for these institutions to maximise student intake while maintaining faculty size and laboratory infrastructure. As of August 21, the NCISM had listed 17 Ayurveda colleges — all private — whose permissions it had denied, several for “non-compliance with inspection process”. In Hillside Ayurveda Medical College (2023), the Karnataka High Court acknowledged that “often educational institutions are … guilty of admitting excess students for financial gains”. The National Commission for Homoeopathy has given 41% of all homoeopathy colleges the lowest grade, including nearly half of all private institutions. Effectively, the expansion of AYUSH education is amid persistent quality issues, including inadequate or disputed faculty strengths, failures in inspection requirements and student intake numbers, and even allegations of fictitious faculty. While it would be premature to infer that the rapid expansion evident will have amplified these problems, the persistent regulatory non-compliance warrants tougher quality control and a reexamination of the incentives for private institutions, together with questions about the evidence backing AYUSH medicinal systems.

editorials.title: Alarm for men's hockey as women up their game
editorials.passage: When the FIH World Cup began at Amstelveen in mid-August, the odds were loaded in favour of India men’s team. When the tournament ended, it was the women’s team that brought solace to the hard-fought campaign. The men’s team, considered a favourite to clinch a medal not long ago, posted a series of disappointing performances that looked insipid—a contrast that will hurt the management the most. The team conceded too many goals and lacked running power in the midfield to control games. An eighth-place finish among 16 competing nations does not look good from any angle, especially for a proud hockey-playing nation with a stellar record.With less than a month to go for the Asian Games, an event where the winners will get an automatic spot at the 2028 Olympics, the side can ill afford to make large-scale changes. Going in with a similar side, they know they will not be seen as the strongest side in the continent despite their FIH ranking. If the World Cup revealed India’s gaps, teams like Pakistan, Malaysia, Japan and South Korea are more than capable of exposing them afresh if given a chance. One thing is sure: if we want another Olympic medal in 2028, the transition has to begin right away.   Even as the men’s team disappointed, the women genuinely surprised many watchers with their defensive discipline, organisation and fitness. Sjoerd Marijne, the Dutch drafted in as coach less than a year ago, has performed a miracle—a fifth-place finish, India’s best since the tournament’s inaugural women’s edition in 1974, where it ended fourth. This could well be the beginning of a new journey for the women’s team. The decision to bring back conditioning guru Wayne Lombard has elevated the side’s fitness a notch. Add to that the exuberance of youth, with 11 first-timers in the 20-member squad, and a side ranked ninth in the world at the start of the tournament could punch well above their weight. By the time they beat Germany 3-1 in the last match, they looked like they belonged in the sport’s upper echelons. The next step in their evolution would be to beat China at the Asian Games. If that happens, it will serve as a major fillip for the women’s game in a country where it’s still struggling to raise interest and funds. .Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Make affordable flu vaccine available to all in National Capital
editorials.passage: The surge in H1N1 viral infections in Delhi this year is strong enough to demand attention. It is not, however, evidence of a new or unusually lethal virus. That distinction matters. The state government put the number of H1N1 cases as of August 27 at 2,729, out of 3,736 influenza A and B cases recorded overall. Influenza A accounted for 3,447 cases, of which H1N1 is a subtype that accounted for almost four-fifths. The H1N1 strain, which has circulated among humans since 2009, has since become established as a seasonal influenza virus.However, the scale and nature of this year’s outbreak makes it stand out. Last year, another influenza A subtype—H3N2—was more prominent in Delhi. And the Indian Council of Medical Research has found no evidence yet of a new threat or an unusual genetic shift in the H1N1 to make it more virulent. That leaves a question Delhi has long been reluctant to confront: why does a city that knows influenza recurs every year continue to treat each rise in cases as an administrative surprise?Influenza viruses keep evolving, making annual vaccination the practical way of reducing the risk of serious illness. The vaccine composition recommended by the World Health Organization for the 2026-27 season in the northern hemisphere includes an updated H1N1 component. It would not prevent every infection, but it can reduce the risk of severe disease, particularly among those most vulnerable. That suggests a policy Delhi should have had years ago: an annual influenza programme, with vaccination offered before the seasonal rise to older people, pregnant women, young children and people with chronic illnesses—accompanied by systematic surveillance. Influenza is usually self-limiting, but in those at risk it can lead to pneumonia, respiratory complications and, in severe cases, hospitalisation or death..However, a second policy question remains. The vaccine’s price is such that access to it cannot be left entirely to the private market. If vaccination is to form part of Delhi’s annual public health strategy, the government must find a way to provide it free to the poorest and most vulnerable, and at subsidised rates to others who cannot afford it. Price should not determine who among those most vulnerable gets protection from serious disease..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | Cleaning up after
editorials.passage: A second fire in two months at the Kodungaiyur dump yard, one of two sites where Chennai’s solid waste is parked, should be taken by all municipalities as a warning. An official of the city’s solid waste management department told this newspaper that methane generated from biodegradable waste had caused the fire that set off noxious fumes affecting several north Chennai localities. It reminds us that India lacks a sustainable policy to manage the immense amounts of solid and liquid waste generated daily by its cities. Technology today allows us to use robotic sorting, biomining, solar-powered compactors and advanced recycling. Not cost—the only thing stopping rich municipalities from managing our waste more efficiently is the apathy of decision makers..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Inherited knowledge
editorials.passage:
A village elder in the Himalayan foothills would watch ants carrying their eggs uphill. To a hurried visitor, it was an ordinary sight. To the elder, it was a warning: heavy rain was approaching. For generations, his community had learned to read such signs ~ the movement of insects, the behaviour of birds, the flowering of particular plants and changes in the wind ~ to anticipate changes in weather. What appeared to be folklore was, in fact, a sophisticated body of environmental knowledge accumulated through centuries of close observation. 

This small anecdote captures the essence of Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS): knowledge born from lived experience, transmitted across generations and deeply embedded in a community’s relationship with nature, society and culture. Today, as the world confronts climate change, biodiversity loss, food insecurity and ecological crises, such knowledge is receiving renewed attention. UNESCO has increasingly recognised that indigenous and local communities are not merely custodians of cultural traditions but important holders of knowledge relevant to some of humanity’s most urgent challenges. 

Indigenous knowledge is often described simply as “traditional knowledge”, but the term encompasses much more. It includes agricultural practices, medicinal knowledge, water management, architecture, weather prediction, biodiversity conservation, food preparation, craftsmanship, oral traditions, languages, rituals and systems of social organisation. Crucially, it is living knowledge. 

It changes as communities respond to new circumstances and environmental conditions. UNESCO’s Local and Indigenous Knowledge Systems (LINKS) programme, established in 2002, seeks to facilitate dialogue between indigenous and local knowledge holders, scientists and policymakers. The programme emphasises that indigenous knowledge can contribute to ecological understanding, environmental policy, biodiversity conservation and sustainable development. The importance of this approach has grown as conventional models of development have come under scrutiny. 

Modern science has enormous explanatory and technological power, but it does not possess a monopoly over knowledge. Indigenous communities have often conducted centuries-long experiments in particular ecosystems ~ without laboratories, computers or sophisticated instruments, but through observation, memory and collective experience. Few countries demonstrate the diversity of indigenous and local knowledge as vividly as India. From the Himalayan mountains to the deserts of Rajasthan, from the forests of central India to the coastal communities of Kerala and Odisha, countless communities have developed practices adapted to their particular ecological and cultural environments. Indian agricultural traditions provide numerous examples. 

Traditional farmers have developed knowledge of seed preservation, mixed cropping, crop rotation, natural pest management and climate-sensitive cultivation. In the dry regions of Rajasthan, traditional systems of harvesting and conserving rainwater demonstrate how communities adapted to severe water scarcity. In the Himalayan region, indigenous building practices have evolved in response to cold, earthquakes and difficult terrain. Similarly, India’s medicinal traditions ~ including Ayurveda and numerous community-based healing practices ~ represent accumulated knowledge of plants and their properties. 

Tribal and forest communities possess detailed knowledge of local flora, food sources and medicinal plants. Such knowledge has enormous cultural and potentially scientific significance. The Indian knowledge landscape also extends beyond material practices. Oral epics, folk songs, dances, festivals, crafts, rituals, storytelling traditions and indigenous languages preserve collective memories and worldviews. UNESCO’s understanding of intangible cultural heritage specifically encompasses oral traditions, performing arts, social practices, rituals, knowledge concerning nature and the universe, and traditional craftsmanship. 

India’s engagement with UNESCO provides an important illustration of how traditional knowledge can acquire international recognition without losing its community-based character. India has ratified the 2003 UNESCO Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, and the country now has 16 elements inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List including Yoga, Kumbh Mela and Durga Puja in Kolkata. These inscriptions are significant not merely because they bring international visibility. They affirm that cultural practices transmitted from generation to generation constitute an important part of humanity's shared heritage. 

Yoga is a particularly striking example. What is now practised globally as a system of physical and mental well-being emerged from a much older Indian philosophical and cultural tradition. Its UNESCO inscription in 2016 illustrates how a practice rooted in a particular civilisation can become part of the world's cultural heritage. Likewise, the traditional brass and copper craftsmanship of the Thatheras of Jandiala Guru demonstrates that indigenous knowledge is not confined to religious or ritual practices. It encompasses specialised technical skills, material knowledge and artisanal expertise transmitted through generations. 

Perhaps the greatest contemporary relevance of Indigenous Knowledge Systems lies in environmental sustainability. Indigenous communities frequently perceive humans as participants within ecosystems rather than masters of nature. Their practices often emphasise restraint, reciprocity and long-term stewardship. UNESCO has observed that indigenous knowledge, grounded in careful observation of ecosystems, can provide valuable insights into sustainability and resilience. Such knowledge is particularly relevant in the context of climate change, biodiversity loss, natural disasters and water insecurity. 

India's own cultural traditions contain numerous examples of ecological sensitivity: sacred groves protected through community beliefs, traditional water-harvesting structures, seasonal agricultural calendars, conservation of indigenous seeds and dietary practices based on locally available resources. These practices should not be romanticised uncritically, but neither should they be dismissed as primitive simply because they predate modern scientific institutions. The real opportunity lies in dialogue between knowledge systems. 

Indigenous knowledge and modern science need not be competitors. Scientific research can test, document and refine traditional practices, while indigenous knowledge can provide scientists with long-term observations and locally grounded insights that are difficult to obtain through short-term research. Yet this knowledge is under threat. Rapid urbanisation, environmental degradation, linguistic erosion, changing lifestyles, commercialisation and the declining transmission of knowledge between generations can cause centuries of accumulated experience to disappear within a few decades. UNESCO notes that traditional knowledge systems are dynamic and living practices, but many are severely endangered. 

Its approach emphasises intergenerational transmission and encourages knowledge-holding communities themselves to lead research and documentation. Language is particularly important. When an indigenous language disappears, an entire conceptual world may disappear with it. Names of plants, ecological classifications, agricultural terminology, medicinal vocabulary and oral histories often have no precise equivalent in another language. UNESCO’s International Decade of Indigenous Languages, 2022-2032, therefore places linguistic preservation at the heart of efforts to safeguard indigenous cultures and knowledge. 

The future of Indigenous Knowledge Systems cannot be limited to putting traditions in museums or archives. The objective should be to keep knowledge alive, useful and community-owned. Schools and universities can play a crucial role by documenting local histories, inviting traditional knowledge holders into classrooms and encouraging students to investigate indigenous environmental practices. Researchers should work with communities rather than merely studying them. Intellectual property and ethical questions must also be addressed so that traditional knowledge is not commercially exploited without recognition, consent or benefit-sharing. 

India has an enormous opportunity here. The country’s educational institutions can connect contemporary scientific education with local ecological knowledge, oral traditions, crafts, agriculture and languages. Such an approach would not mean rejecting modern science. Rather, it would create a richer intellectual environment in which different ways of knowing can interact. UNESCO’s recent work makes an important point: indigenous peoples should be recognised not simply as subjects of cultural preservation but as knowledge holders and active partners in building resilience. Its 2025 publication Indigenous Knowledge, Ancestral Places: Navigating Change in UNESCO Designated Sites highlights how indigenous communities continue to adapt ancestral knowledge to contemporary challenges. 


The world may therefore have to rediscover what that Himalayan elder already knew: knowledge is not always found in books, laboratories or databases. Sometimes it resides in a song, a seed, a craft technique, the design of a village pond, the memory of an elderly farmer or the careful observation of an insect. For India, Indigenous Knowledge Systems are not merely relics of the past. They are part of a living intellectual inheritance ~ and potentially an important resource for the future. UNESCO’s growing recognition of this fact offers an opportunity to move beyond the old opposition between “modern” and “traditional” knowledge. 

The real challenge is to create a dialogue between them, ensuring that ancient wisdom is neither frozen in the past nor exploited in the present, but allowed to contribute meaningfully to a more sustainable and culturally diverse future. In an age increasingly dominated by artificial intelligence and digital technologies, perhaps the most valuable lesson of Indigenous Knowledge Systems is surprisingly simple: before we learn how to control nature, we must learn how to listen to it. 

(The writer is Assistant Professor in English, Pritilata Waddedar Mahavidyalaya, Nadia)

editorials.title: Some positives from India-China talks
editorials.passage:
India’s National Security Advisor Ajit Doval held the 25th round of Special Representative (SR) talks with his counterpart, Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi, in Beijing last week. The talks came about a month before the BRICS summit, which Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to attend, though confirmation is yet to be received. Meanwhile an advance delegation from China is in New Delhi, working on hotel arrangements and security protocol for Xi. This will be Xi’s first visit post the Galwan clash. He had last visited India in 2019. The SR talks were held shortly after India released its own list of names for places in Arunachal Pradesh, to which China objected. 

It does appear that the Chinese tended to downplay the impact of the Indian action, though aware that it challenges their claims on Arunachal and could spread to other sectors. It also appears that the two sides are attempting to stabilize ties, despite differences over border alignment and regional security. It was for this reason that the word ‘delimitation’ was used in the joint statement, issued 24 hours after the meeting. The terms in use earlier were border management or disengagement. These implied short-term management, but delimitation indicates the intent to move towards a permanent settlement. 

The meeting led to the issuance of ‘eight points of outcomes and consensus.’ Amongst the eight, a few are significant. The first is continuing discussions on “Early and Substantial Harvest of boundary delimitation and Border Management.’ This implies resolving border issues region by region, rather than as a whole. Maps had been exchanged on the Middle Sector, but further movement was stalled. India had for long been against partial border settlement but appears to have accepted this approach. This was first discussed positively by the two sides at a similar meeting in August last year. 

It also added that an Expert Group on Boundary Delimitation and a Working Group on Border Management will have to first agree on respective terms of reference. While the process would still be slow, it is a positive trend. The first two regions which could come under resolution would be Sikkim and the Central Sector, comprising Uttarakhand and Himachal, where differences are minimal. Two additional meeting points and hot lines, one each for the Eastern and Central sector, were agreed upon. The two sides also announced that any ‘situation on the ground’ would be addressed through existing diplomatic and military channels. These channels include the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination, local commander-level meetings etc. 

The intent appears to keep the situation along the borders stable. The selected locations for meeting points should be accessible to both sides by proper roads and be on or close to the border. Final names will be released once accepted by both sides. Another aspect was agreeing to hold the next meeting of the Expert-level Mechanism on Trans-border Rivers in September this year. This is aimed at maintaining communication on issues including sharing hydrological data. This particularly impacts the Brahmaputra flowing from Tibet. India’s concerns stem from flood management and implications from China’s construction of major hydropower projects in the upper basins. 

Timely data is crucial for disaster preparedness and water security. Simultaneously, there has been an increase in numbers attending the Kailash Manasarovar Yatra, and three additional trading points have been opened. The two sides have also moved forward in a number of spheres. India has permitted investors from countries bordering India to acquire up to 10 per cent non-controlling stake in all, less restricted sectors. Tourist visas and direct flights have also resumed. Visas for journalists remain a pending issue. However, distr ust continues. Differences in claim lines, largely in Arunachal and Ladakh result occasionally in prolonged standoffs as happened in July this year. 

Though there have been no clashes since Yangtze in December 2022, they could occur unless checked. Additional hotlines and meeting points could possibly diffuse the scenario before it escalates. On its part, China is concerned about India’s growing ties with Japan, especially the recently inked memorandum on maritime security co op eration, coming when China-Japan ties are sliding. Added is India’s membership of the QUAD, which China has always believed was aimed at it. It is India which is against its militarization. With US focus shifting, QUAD currently is on low key. 

China’s open support to Pakistan, as evident during Operation Sindoor last year, is an indicator that while it may ‘stabilize’ its border with India, it will exploit Pakistan as a proxy. It will also continue to use Pakistan as a testing ground for its military products. The other concern is the growing technological gap between India and China in almost all fields, largely military. This will impact India’s defence preparedness. To display positivity and create a congenial atmosphere, the wording in the joint statement said: “The two sides agreed to strengthen exchanges and cooperation in border trade, pilgrimage and other areas, with the view to work together to create an atmosphere featuring dialogue, peace, consultation and cooperation in the border areas.” 

The timing of the SR talks are also very relevant. The forthcoming BRICS summit is important for multiple reasons and hence it was essential for India and China to display unity. Firstly, India will be handing over the baton for the next summit to China, which will assume the presidency from 1 January 2027. If Xi does not attend in Delhi, Modi might hesitate next year. Secondly, the summit is at a time when Trump is increasing his economic measures against countries trading with Iran and Russia. India and China are two nations in Trump’s crosshairs. Thirdly, it is also time for BRICS to send the right message to the US. The presence of the Iranian and Russian Presidents, Masoud Pezeshkian and Vladimir Putin, at the summit would indicate that the grouping has unity. 

The absence of Xi would display disunity within the BRICS. Fourthly, major powers attending the summit would highlight close cooperation amongst the leaders of the global South. Finally, what remains crucial is India’s diplomatic heft to issue a joint declaration at the end of the BRICS summit. The Doval-Xi summit was also positively projected in Chinese media, conveying that China is seeking far more than just border management. It hopes that high-level communication channels between India and China continue. The next step to watch in the process is the Xi-Modi summit. What flows from it would convey the future direction of relations between the two sides. 

(The writer is a retired Major-General of the Indian Army)

editorials.title: Hubris cannot rewrite laws of nature
editorials.passage:
How do you explain what Charles Dickens called “the best of times, and the worst of times?” We live today with massive social inequalities. The rich never had it so good; the middle class was never so discontented, consecutive years of heat waves, wars in two continents, stock markets at record high and bond markets suffering from four-decade high interest rates. 

Are we going through imperial over-stretch or simply over-stretched asset valuations? Across centuries and civilizations, macro-historians of war and empires shared a remarkably similar view: societies thrive when their values, economies, and institutions remain anchored to physical reality but decay when elites drift into self-referential systems of paper wealth, prestige, and power. Climate change, fossil fuels, water, food and energy are anchored physically to the laws of thermodynamics, whereas human perception and agency (the willingness to intervene in human affairs and nature) can be detached from reality by ego, hubris and euphoria. 

The three laws of thermodynamics, which proved universal for all systems are first, law of energy conservation - energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another; second on entropy and irreversibility - in any spontaneous process, the total entropy (disorder) of the universe always increases, and third on absolute zero - as the temperature of a system approaches absolute zero, the entropy of the system approaches a minimum constant value. 

This means that absolute zero cannot be reached. Strictly sp eaking , the laws of thermodynamics do not apply to human social systems, since human perceptions or valuations can b e inflated or understated, somewhat detached from reality, whilst human agency changes the game. Just as AI models hallucinate, humans’ perception or valuation of assets go from mild inflation to periodic hallucination with great crashes, the last in October 1929 that led to the Great Depression and ultimately the Second World War. The view that the Soviet system collapsed because it violated the ‘hard budget constraint’ was originated by Hungarian economist János Kornai (1928–2021). He saw market economy firms that go bankrupt when they consistently lose money as a hard budget constraint. 

This imposes discipline and drives efficiency. In the Soviet socialist system, state-owned enterprises and governments operated under soft budget constraints because the state would bail out losers until the state itself became bankrupt, default or collapse. Hard-budget constraints are thermodynamic limits on fiscal excesses. Cambridge political economist Helen Thompson was the first to draw parallels between geopolitics of war and energy, highlighting that the Ukraine war was really about food, energy (and also rare minerals). Political, military, money and social power run on energy. No more energy or money, the system stops or declines. 

Western macro-historians like Arnold Toynbee or Harvard’s Paul Kennedy argued that empires rise through creative adaptation and shared purpose, then rot as elites become self-serving, overextending militarily while their economic core hollows out. As complexity increases, new laws and bigger bureaucracies cost more money, resources or energy than the system can bear. When elites fail to respond to crises with no more surplus left, the system collapses. These insights are not uniquely Western. Fourteenth-century Arab scholar Ibn Khaldūn captured the full lifecycle in a single concept: ‘asabiyyah’-shared cohesion and purpose. 

Empires rise lean, grow fat on luxury and bureaucracy, then starve as taxes crush the productive base and elites lose the will to adapt. Ancient India’s Kautilya put it bluntly: wealth is the foundation of power. Surplus comes first; everything else follows. Paper prestige cannot feed an army or sustain an empire. Chinese traditions, meanwhile, frame the challenge as alignment with nature. Do not force what cannot succeed - act with reality, not against it. With experience of numerous rises and falls of dynasties, pragmatism, not ideology, becomes the survival strategy: test small, adjust, scale, and never mistake names for substance. 

Across all these traditions, one lesson remains: moral order and physical order are one. Hard budget constraints, justice and shared purpose are not luxuries; they lower enforcement costs, sustain trust, and conserve energy. When the moral anchor fails, the thermodynamic collapse follows. Today, as fund manager Ray Dalio sees it, the global order displays late-stage symptoms. All governments are running debt burdens faster than real output; financial engineering outpaces productive engineering; reserve currency privilege lets consumption run ahead of natural resources. Narratives and memes amplify faster than facts; markets value acceleration over substance. 

We are not witnessing the “end of history.” We are essentially watching the thermodynamic bill come due. Every financial transaction, every institution, every army runs on real energy and resources. Charles Dickens’ novel David Copperfield (1850) summed it up best: “Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure nineteen nineteen and six, result happiness. 

Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure twenty pounds ought and six, result misery.” Humans prosper when we stay grounded in reality. We fall when we believe hubris can rewrite the laws of nature. Markets that are concentrated and over-stretched in valuation are fragile, whose bursting will have systemic implications. Facing such reality is not a policy choice, but admitting the hard knocks of life. 

(The writer is Adjunct Professor at Tsinghua University, Beijing and University of Malaya, and former Chairman of the Securities and Futures Commission, Hong Kong)

editorials.title: Bangladesh Test
editorials.passage:
India’s eagerness to host Tarique Rahman is about more than diplomatic courtesy. It reflects a harder reality: New Delhi has lost the strategic certainty it once enjoyed in Dhaka and is now trying to rebuild influence without the political conditions that made its relationship with former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina so comfortable. The temptation in Delhi may be to see Rahman’s visit as a reset button. It is not. Bangladesh has changed, its politics have changed, and its expectations of India have changed. 

Any durable relationship will have to be negotiated on new terms. Hasina’s presence in India is the immediate obstacle. Dhaka’s demand for her extradition is not simply a legal request. It has become a test of whether India recognises the political transformation that followed her removal. Her decision to address Bangladesh from Indian soil has made the problem more difficult. Whatever Delhi’s legal position, Dhaka can interpret the continued presence and public activity of its former leader as evidence that India has not fully adjusted to the new political reality. 

That creates a dilemma for Rahman. Visiting Delhi is in Bangladesh’s interest. India is too important a neighbour to ignore, particularly when trade, energy, water, border management, connectivity and access to the northeastern states are involved. But Rahman cannot afford to appear dependent on India, especially after winning power in a political environment shaped by resentment of Hasina’s long partnership with Delhi. India therefore needs to understand that the old bargain cannot simply be restored. Under Hasina, security cooperation and connectivity expanded because both governments saw strategic advantage in close alignment. 

But that alignment also generated a perception in Bangladesh that India was willing to overlook democratic and human-rights concerns for the sake of a friendly government. Rebuilding trust will require more than ceremonial honours. The Pakistan factor makes the stakes higher. Bangladesh’s renewed military and diplomatic engagement with Islamabad is a reminder that Dhaka now has more room to diversify its relationships. India need not view every Bangladeshi opening to Pakistan as a strategic threat, but it cannot assume that geography alone will guarantee Indian primacy. 

The answer is not to demand loyalty from Dhaka. It is to make partnership with India demonstrably useful. That means treating Bangladesh as a sovereign neighbour whose interests sometimes diverge from India’s, while protecting India’s own core concerns on security, connectivity and the border. It also means separating long-term bilateral interests from the unresolved fate of Hasina. 

Extradition may be a difficult legal and political question; the broader relationship cannot remain permanently hostage to it. Rahman’s visit, if it happens, should therefore be judged not by the grandeur of his welcome but by what follows. Can the two governments establish a relationship based on reciprocity rather than old political alignments? For India, that is the real test. The objective should not be to recover the Bangladesh of the Hasina years. It should be to build a relationship with the Bangladesh that exists now.

editorials.title: Dolly’s Lesson
editorials.passage:
Dolly Parton’s death leaves America with an uncomfortable question: what happens to a public culture when almost every prominent figure is expected to choose a political side? Parton became extraordinary not because she was above politics, but because she understood that public influence did not require partisan combat. She could hold convictions without turning every conviction into a loyalty test. 

In a country increasingly organised around political identity, that was a rare form of power. Her appeal crossed boundaries that American politics routinely treats as irreconcilable. Conservatives could admire her without feeling that they were surrendering their politics. Liberals could embrace her without requiring a political declaration. Religious Americans, LGBTQ audiences, feminists, country traditionalists and younger generations could all find something of themselves in her. That did not happen because she stood for nothing. 

It happened because she did not reduce herself to one thing. The distinction is important. Parton avoided partisan politics, but she was not morally silent. Her support for women's equality, LGBTQ people and racial causes demonstrated that refusing to campaign for a party need not mean refusing to recognise injustice. Her preferred language was often generosity rather than confrontation. That approach matters beyond celebrity culture. Modern political communication increasingly rewards outrage. Politicians, activists and even entertainers are encouraged to identify enemies, announce allegiances and turn audiences into ideological communities. 

Social media makes the process profitable: anger travels faster than nuance, and denunciation often produces greater engagement than persuasion. Parton offered a different model. She built trust before asking people to listen. Her humour lowered defences. Her songs dealt with poverty, ambition, insecurity, work, love and discrimination without requiring listeners to pass an ideological examination. Her philanthropy, particularly her vast children's literacy programme, translated celebrity into something concrete: books, opportunity and access. There was another lesson in her career. Behind the extravagant appearance was a woman fiercely protective of independence. 

She understood that creative control was economic power. Her decision to retain ownership of her songwriting rights, even when doing so meant turning down the opportunity to have Elvis Presley record one of her songs, eventually proved enormously consequential. That combination ~ personal independence, commercial intelligence and social generosity ~ may be Parton’s most enduring legacy. She did not preach against the American Dream; she complicated it. She showed that becoming wealthy need not end the obligation to give something back, and that self-interest and social responsibility need not be enemies. America does not need celebrities to replace politicians. 

Nor should public figures be expected to remain silent about injustice. But Parton’s life suggests that there is a political value in refusing to make every human relationship partisan. In a fractured society, the rarest public figure may be one who can make people feel included without first asking which side they are on. Parton managed that. Her real achievement was not making America agree with her. It was making disagreement seem less important than the things people could still share.

editorials.title: Inverted House
editorials.passage:
There is a difference between watching Parliament live on television and watching it from inside. Let me confess that the picture is far more complicated — and, at times, much more amusing — when viewed from inside. I entered Parliament after 36 years in the police service, and my first parliamentary session has been an education of a different kind.

Both Houses met for 19 days during the recent Monsoon session amid repeated disruptions. Several Bills were passed without meaningful participation by members, and Question Hour functioned for only a fraction of its allotted time.

We often speak of the four pillars of democracy — legislature, executive, judiciary and the press. Our Constitution does not place them in any neat hierarchy. Yet, having adopted a parliamentary form of government, Parliament occupies a ‘first among equals’ place. After attending my first session in Parliament, I find myself wondering whether that position has quietly been turned upside down.

The government places a legislation before the House, the Treasury benches support it, the Opposition opposes it, and the result is usually known even before the debate begins. The executive is born from Parliament and is supposed to remain accountable to it. Yet, increasingly, the relationship has started to look like the other way round. At times, Parliament looks less like the institution holding the executive to account and more like Dhritarashtra blindly indulging every demand of his sons out of misguided affection.

A government with a majority is, of course, entitled to pass its legislative programme. But surely, Parliament was intended to do more than provide numerical certification. How often does a minister, after listening to members, stand up and say: ‘That is a fair point. We will amend the Bill.’

I learnt my own small lessons in this. I had prepared a Question Hour intervention on the absence of any upper limit on surging domestic airfares. The government itself caps dynamic pricing for app-based cabs like Uber, Rapido, Yatri Sathi and so on. Yet airline ticket prices can rise dramatically when demand peaks. The airfare cap was removed in March 2026. My question was quite simple: if we believe that a cab aggregator should not be free to charge an unlimited surge fare, why should there not be a comparable safeguard for airline passengers? The question could not be asked even though it did make it to the starred questions list. Sometimes the questions Parliament fails to ask tell us more about its condition.

I did, however, get an opportunity to speak on two Bills.

The first was the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026. A leaked examination paper is like robbing a young person of an opportunity. What is stolen is not merely a question paper; it is time, opportunity and faith in the fairness of the system. The government’s answer lay in the severity of punishment — longer imprisonment, higher fines and strict timelines. One lesson my long service in policing has taught me — criminology supports this — is that it is the certainty of punishment, not merely its quantum, that deters crime. A leak mafia does not consult the penal schedule before stealing a question paper. It calculates the probability of being caught. What troubled me more was that Parliament had already studied this problem in detail. A Standing Committee had pointed to dependence on outside vendors, blacklisted firms securing work elsewhere, and the need for greater transparency. But many of its recommendations were not implemented. If committees spend months examining a subject, the executive should explain why important recommendations are rejected or left unimplemented; otherwise scrutiny by parliamentary committees loses its meaning.

I welcomed the setting up of the task force headed by Nandan Nilekani. But I wondered why the government could not have waited for its recommendations before bringing the amendment Bill. If the task force now proposes changes requiring legislative backing, will the government move another Bill to amend the law yet again? During the debate, I asked members on the Treasury benches to keep their government hat aside for a moment and think as members of the legislature — but in vain. In a matter involving our sons and daughters, if we cannot think in a bipartisan manner, when shall we?

The second Bill — Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026 — increased the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court. But I asked the House to consider the poor state of the justice delivery system. Across my policing career, I have repeatedly seen people walk into police stations with bounced-cheque disputes, landlord-tenant disagreements, and other civil matters. They come to police stations not because they have great faith in the police but because they have far less faith in the judicial process. The system urgently needs fixing. India does not merely need more judges. The Supreme Court Collegium has the decisive role in recommending who those judges should be even though the Constitution contains no word called ‘collegium’. India needs faster, affordable and accessible justice. Judicial independence is non-negotiable. But judicial independence and judicial primacy in appointments, judicial administration and justice delivery are not necessarily the same thing. A near-complete judicial primacy raises its own questions related to transparency and accountability.

An uneasy truce prevails. The judiciary, understandably, guards its independence. Yet the painfully slow pace of justice does not appear to receive the same urgency. The executive pushes back from time to time. Parliament, which should provide the democratic forum for discussion of such issues, largely watches from the sidelines. This is where democracy begins to look upside down.

Coming back to the four pillars of democracy — the executive must govern; the judiciary must protect the Constitution; the press must question us all. But Parliament must deliberate, scrutinise and hold everyone accountable. Parliament possesses something no other institution does: the democratic legitimacy of citizens speaking through their elected representatives. That legitimacy should not be trivialised or reduced to a headcount.

There is, of course, a side of Parliament the cameras rarely catch. Members who were tearing into one another on the floor of the House can be found at the same table in the parliamentary canteen exchanging jokes and comparing notes on constituency problems. I do not see this bonhomie as hypocrisy. Politics needs disagreement but it can do without dislike. This leaves me with one question: if we can listen to one another over a cup of coffee, why do we find it so hard to do so on the floor of the House?

After one session, I certainly do not claim to have the answers. I have, however, acquired quite a few questions. For a new parliamentarian, perhaps that is not a bad start.

Rajeev Kumar is a member of the Rajya Sabha. Views expressed in the article are personal.

editorials.title: The medium has changed
editorials.passage:
Separated by little more than three weeks, two exits tell one story. The former Union education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, stepped down after months of student-led fury over irregularities in examinations. Next, the Bharatiya Janata Party quietly retired its social media chief, Amit Malviya. Read together, they signal that India’s political communication ecosystem is entering a new phase.

For over a decade, analysts have treated social media as an auxiliary tool of electoral politics — useful, but secondary. But that framing is starting to feel dated because it continues to treat platforms as tools rather than environments. Tools help you do politics. Environments shape what politics even looks like.

The BJP grasped this distinction earlier than its competitors did. Its 2014 campaign treated Facebook, WhatsApp, and television not as channels for transmitting messages but as a new communicative infrastructure altogether. By 2019, that had matured into an entire ecosystem — ad spending, data analytics, content production, coordinated outreach, the works.

Most of the existing literature looks at this shift through campaign spending, Twitter activity, Facebook networks, and voting behaviour. More recent work has widened the lens to include influencers and short-form video as well as meme creators as political actors in their own right. But even this scholarship has spent less time on something more basic: the slow transition from party-controlled communication to communication controlled by creators.

That’s where Instagram becomes politically interesting. Unlike Facebook and television, its organising principle isn’t broadcasting — it is recommendation. Television sends the same content to millions of people at once. Facebook works through networks, groups, and personal connections. Instagram functions through algorithmic discovery: people encounter political content not because they went looking for it but because the platform decided to show it to them.

That difference matters because every platform rewards a different style of communication. Television rewards authority and repetition; Facebook rewards networks and community; Instagram rewards emotional resonance, visual storytelling, and cultural relevance. And political speech on Instagram isn’t bound by the conventions that shape a television debate or a newspaper editorial. A parliamentary speech becomes a reel. A government report becomes an infographic. A protest slogan becomes a meme. And sometimes, a meme becomes a movement. The Cockroach Janta Party is probably the clearest example of this so far. The CJP didn’t sustain itself despite Instagram — it sustained itself because of Instagram. Every reel kept the protest alive a little longer. Every repost renewed its visibility. Every meme turned private frustration into something collective.

Moreover, the movement also showed that digital participation can’t be dismissed as a performative act any longer. For years, people have talked about online activism and street politics as if they belong in separate boxes. That distinction is looking increasingly artificial. Street politics gives a movement legitimacy: digital politics gives it reach. The future of mobilisation probably belongs to movements that do both at once.

That’s a problem for Opposition parties. For most of the past decade, Opposition politics has swung between two flawed strategies. One is sticking with the old instruments — press conferences, marches, public meetings, parliamentary interventions. The other is trying to copy the BJP’s digital playbook through IT cells and reactive social media campaigns. Neither is working particularly well.

The Opposition’s mistake has been assuming digital politics is something that can be handed off to a communications team. That misreads what these platforms actually are. Instagram isn’t the digital wing of a party: it’s a creator ecosystem with its own rules entirely, and those rules favour authenticity over institutional messaging, participation over broadcasting, cultural production over political formality.

So Opposition parties need to stop trying to replicate what worked before. Recreating the BJP’s 2014 playbook for 2029 would mean preparing for yesterday’s war while today’s is already underway. What they need instead is decentralised creator networks independent of party structure. Political communication can’t stay confined to spokespersons and official handles anymore. Educators, satirists, regional creators, comedians, podcasters, student groups, and independent commentators are already shaping how younger audiences think about politics. This also means rethinking what a protest even is. Every physical movement needs a digital strategy running alongside it. Every demonstration should generate creator-led content. Every march should leave behind a visual archive. Every campaign should be producing reels, memes, explainers, podcasts, and decentralised user-generated content.

Influencers, meme creators, and short-form content are shaping democratic discourse in a serious way. What hasn’t quite sunk in yet is the fuller implication: we’re watching creators compete with parties for public attention, algorithms compete with editors for agenda-setting power, and cultural production compete with ideology as the dominant way politics actually persuades people.

That might be why the recent reshuffle in the BJP’s digital operation drew so much attention. Personnel changes are rarely just about the individual involved — they often signal that an organisation has quietly concluded that its old model has run its course.

Marshall McLuhan once said the medium is the message. In India today, that idea probably needs updating. The platform isn’t just the medium through which politics gets communicated anymore. Increasingly, it decides how politics gets imagined, performed, consumed, and fought over in the first place.

Saqib Parvaiz Yetoo is a Srinagar-based researcher

editorials.title: Fight differently
editorials.passage:
The Crime in India report by the National Crime Records Bureau reveals a worrying trend in drug law enforcement. In 2022, 2023, and 2024, around 115,000, 120,000, and 109,000 cases were registered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act. Among these registered cases, trafficking cases numbered 38,000, 41,000, and 37,000, respectively, whereas consumption cases were 77,000, 78,000, and 72,000, respectively. Broadly speaking, of all registered cases during these three years, one-third related to trafficking while two-thirds related to the consumption of substances criminalised under Section 27 of the NDPS Act. So, two-thirds of all registered NDPS cases of 2024 targeted individual users rather than traffickers or drug supply chains.

Since nearly all cases under the NDPS Act are registered on the initiative of drug law enforcement agencies, this lopsided ratio raises four critical concerns for our criminal justice framework.

Firstly, it demonstrates that law enforcement resources are disproportionately directed towards drug consumption rather than trafficking. Second, such a large number of consumption cases chokes the legal system. Limited investigative resources — forensic labs, investigators, equipment, and tools — as well as prosecution and trial resources, which should focus on trafficking, are frittered away on minor users. Third, a study by the Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy indicated systemic misuse of Section 27 by the police. Fourth, this fuels severe overcrowding of prisons.

Consumption of substances is primarily a public health issue and not a criminal justice issue. While Section 64A of the NDPS Act provides for “Immunity from prosecution to people with an addiction, volunteering for treatment”, it has three structural limitations.

First, the sequence of action is as follows. The case is detected/registered; the person with an addiction is arrested and forwarded to court, then to jail. Later, the person can be offered the option of deaddiction treatment instead of prosecution. By then, it may be too late. Jail exposes the person with an addiction to traffickers and hardened criminals, sometimes facilitating their transition from addiction to trafficking. Second, for all practical purposes, Section 64A of the NDPS Act is a dead letter. In a pioneering field study on the working of the NDPS Act in Punjab, “From Addict to Convict”, Neha Singhal and her colleagues found that in thousands of such consumption cases, this provision was not successfully invoked even once during 2013-15. Thirdly, a criminal record in our system is a big stigma. When the NDPS Act was enacted, criminalisation of consumption was widespread. But the world has moved forward. In most of western Europe and North America, the consumption of substances has been decriminalised. Portugal pioneered this shift, resulting in a dramatic drop in drug-related HIV transmissions, fewer overdose deaths, and reduced youth abuse rates. Many other European countries quickly followed Portugal. Criminalisation of consumption has been replaced by non-criminal sanctions, ranging from fines to suspension of passports and driving licences. However, trafficking, by and large, remains a criminal offence.

Closer home, the Sikkim Anti-Drugs Act treats consumption primarily as a public health issue rather than a criminal justice issue. It provides individuals two opportunities to reform and uses criminal sanctions for the third offence only. In contrast, Section 27 of the NDPS Act does not even distinguish between habitual users and a first-time experimenter. SADA looks at drug traffickers and individuals struggling with substance use disorder through totally different lenses.

There is thus a need to re-evaluate our approach towards the menace of drugs. Progress lies in treating substance use as a public health issue and decriminalising personal consumption.

Abhay is former DGP Odisha and former Director General, Narcotics Control Bureau

editorials.title: Join hands: Editorial on Nepal floods and the need for transnational cooperation
editorials.passage:
Nepal, besieged by a natural calamity, continues to draw the attention of the subcontinent and much of the world. The death toll from the glacial collapse that led to the flood of mud and sludge that devastated Nepal continues to climb: the 900-mark has been breached even as thousands remain missing. A causal analysis of the devastation has led the proverbial compass to point at the spectre of glacial lake outburst flood events. The relevant data are chilling. Glaciers are spread across 48,000 square kilometres across the Himalayas, including 5,000 glacial lakes: of these, 500 are believed to be hazardous. Their risk has been aggravated by the corresponding rise in climate change-induced glacial loss. Estimates suggest that there has been a fivefold rise in GLOF events after 1950. Significantly, India has suffered the highest number of deaths from glacial floods — the trigger of the Nepal tragedy. It ranks third among the eight nations in the Hindu Kush-Himalayas region when it comes to suffering deluges of this kind. The factors are not far to seek. They include not just extreme weather events facilitated by changing climate but also the pursuit of a faulty development model in higher altitudes along with reckless tourism and wilful degradation of local ecologies. Worse, these frequent calamities can no longer be treated as isolated episodes. They will form a part of a long and crippling chain of destruction as the Himalayas enter an unstable phase.

One aspect that has come to light in this context is the need for transnational cooperation among afflicted nation-states. This is, as environmental organisations stated last week, the need of the hour and must include the establishment of a shared network to facilitate real-time monitoring of not only risky glaciers but also unstable rivers, slopes, valleys and suchlike. The installation of early warning systems, collation and sharing of data as well as joint scientific expeditions must also be part of this deterrence plan. But geostrategic impulses continue to pose the most significant challenge to such transboundary cooperation. For instance, China and India — their diplomatic ties are often prickly — can do a lot more in terms of cooperation on the environmental front. China has also been accused by Tibet of concealing the scale of the current catastrophe. Nations will do well to remember that prioritising strategic compulsions in the face of Armageddon cannot be described as myopia: it is lunacy.

editorials.title: Endless war: Editorial on Iran conflict and limits of American power
editorials.passage:
Six months after the United States of America and Israel launched an unprovoked war on Iran, an old truism on military conflicts is proving to be right, yet again: it is far easier to start a fight than to end one. History’s most powerful military bombed vast parts of Iran, killing its Supreme Leader and thousands of people but its goals — military, political and diplomatic — remain elusive. The US president, Donald Trump, spoke of a regime change aided by Iranians. Instead, the theocratic leadership of Iran, backed by the military, appears to have strengthened its grip over the country. Within days of the start of the war, Mr Trump and other senior members of his administration insisted that they had decimated Iran’s military, especially its navy. Yet Iran maintains a chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz, launching missiles at American bases in the region: Tehran struck the United Arab Emirates and Jordan on Monday morning after the US attacked Iran’s Larak island. Mr Trump has also failed to secure support for his war from any of Washington’s major allies.

Iran has suffered the most from this war: its schoolchildren have been massacred by the US and Israel, its research centres and universities bombed, and its already fragile economy is in a deeper crisis. Yet Iran has shown that in a world where even the pretence of international law has vanished, it is still able to inflict enough pain on its adversaries. Rising energy prices have led to inflation globally, including in the US. The war is unpopular in the US and could cost Mr Trump’s Republican Party the majority in the Congress in the mid-term polls. It has dramatically depleted the US’s weapons inventory, exposing Washington’s limitations in waging a long war. What has eroded simultaneously is the US’s legacy as a protector in the Gulf neighbours. Consequently, fresh defence alliances have emerged: these will have regional ramifications. Countries around the world have started thinking of new ways to source and store energy, food and fertilisers as a buffer against such conflicts. Six months after Mr Trump tried to demolish Iran, it is American credibility that stands shattered.

editorials.title: Middle class mobility vs the K-shaped ghost
editorials.passage:
After a sterling performance in the post-pandemic period, India went through a cyclical slowdown in 2024 and then a series of external shocks originating in US policy. Whenever the economy faces some issues, analysis that sees serious internal flaws as holding the economy back resurfaces and gains attention. Continual outperformance does discredit opportunistic analysis. Even so, let us examine the K-shaped ghost that keeps popping up.

When the fall in poverty could not be disputed any longer, critics moved to inequality. The pandemic recovery was said to be K-shaped, income growth was poor and therefore consumption was unsustainable. Aggregate consumption, however, recovered to show healthy growth. Rural migrants, with rising incomes in lower quartiles, drove a boom in smaller cities.

When extreme poverty based on World Bank figures of those earning less than ₹62 a day has fallen from about 30 per cent to 5 per cent of a 1.4 billion population, it has to imply a large rise in lower middle class income and population.

But the current revival of the K-shaped ghost says the middle class is stagnant, with no rise in numbers or in per capita incomes. For example, Saurabh Mukherjee et al (SM) in their recent book define 40 million taxpayers in the slab between ₹5 lakh and ₹1 crore till 2023 as the middle class. They argue this is stagnant since 2019.

But since very few pay income tax in India because of all kinds of exemptions and a periodic rise in lower limits, this seriously underestimates the middle class. The World Inequality Lab report (Picketty and co-authors) made the same mistake of over-reliance of tax data, for which it was widely criticised. It may be a valid methodology for the US where tax data capture about 80 per cent of income, but not for India where it is about 20 per cent. Notice also that 2019-23 is the period when recovery from the pandemic was just beginning.

Even if numbers in an arbitrarily defined income range, show little change, this does not imply stagnancy. Static numbers can hide large churn as people move through income distributions. If entry and exit are equal, numbers can be constant even as those who enter from lower income ranges and those who exit to higher income ranges are all becoming richer.

But SM numbers are also contestable. Most global and Indian estimates give about one-third of the population, which exceeds 400 million, as middle class. PRICE’s extensive survey-based research defines middle class as incomes from ₹5 lakh to ₹30 lakh. This grew by about 100 million in the last 10 years. Their upper middle class and rich count, with income above ₹30 lakh, is 56 million. Compared to SM’s 40 million, their estimate of people with income exceeding ₹5 lakh is 487 million individuals or about 100 million households!

A Bombay University study finds similar figures. These estimates do much better than the Picketty or SM estimates on simple consistency checks like matching per capita income derived from the income distributions with the aggregate estimated per capita income, consumption or savings. With India’s growth rates it is not possible that the middle class is stagnant.

SM indulge in other factual cherry picking. They find inflation to be higher for this class but ignore the sharp fall in Indian retail inflation compared to a decade ago; their non-housing debt is said to be highest in the world, ignoring that Indian private debt ratios are still lower than most global peers, credit card growth has stabilised, banks are lending more to households that include small firms since they are lending less to large corporates; they point to retail losses in futures trading, ignoring wealth created through mutual funds and other stable investments. Moreover, the switch from earlier informal trading venues is enabling regulatory interventions.

But their advice to the Indian middle class — give up on an India that is neglecting you and invest abroad through funds SM’s company floats is the most suspect! Unfortunately for the sales pitch, instead foreign funds are returning to Indian markets as the AI play loses steam and large government debt weighs on foreign markets.

While the analysis may be flawed it has resonated because it is true that jobs and wages need to rise much faster in India in order to match rising aspirations, as our restless Gen Z reminds us. It is easy to whip up resentment when others seem to be doing better than we are.

But Indian statistics show typical features of catch-up growth in a large labour surplus country. A billion people cannot all become rich overnight.

While unorganised sector real wage growth is flat, corporate nominal wage growth exceeds inflation at about 10 per cent per year. But firms’ profits and savings are growing much faster. In surplus labour economies unskilled wages tend to be low until the surplus is absorbed.

Even so, growth does deliver better jobs in time. A number of databases on formal and informal employment available now show this. Wages are rising fastest for casual work, suggesting shortages in this category. Gig work offers a useful top-up.

The best strategy to earn more is to acquire skills in short supply. In India unfortunately there is a mismatch between education and job skills because of an excess of undergraduate degrees. Youth unemployment since the 1980s is high below the age of 30 and falls after, partly because of the tendency to keep trying for scarce and secure government jobs.

There is a large increase in the number educational and training institutions but it is not so easy to raise quality as quickly. Many improvements in governance are possible with decentralised competition. That students are agitating for better quality should produce results since the polity responds to voter pressure.

But new technologies give students powerful weapons to raise and calibrate their skills to high-wage jobs becoming available. They can find the best teaching resources as well as AI tutors online, to compensate for whatever is lacking in their own institutions. I am often impressed by the skill sets of students who write to me from remote universities. Employers now tend to look at skills rather than degrees.

Better allocation and higher productivity pave the way for wage growth. There are signs that productivity is improving. The CIEC calculates annual labour productivity growth from real GDP and annual employment. While the average from December 1992 to December 2025 is 2.65 per cent YoY, it was 4.82 per cent in 2024 and 8.93 in 2025, exceeding China’s 6.31 per cent that year. All productivity measures tend to rise in higher growth periods.

For policymakers, therefore, the best strategy is to ignore attempts to raise old ghosts and remain laser-focused on sustaining India’s catch-up growth despite external shocks, by increasing diversity and relieving supply-side bottlenecks including in skilling. But students also have the tools to better match their skills with growing opportunities.

The writer is President, TIES, and Professor Emeritus, IGIDR

Published on September 1, 2026

editorials.title: The anatomy of US public debt
editorials.passage:
The US government, the world’s media declares, is mired in debt with the volume of debt crossing a record $4 trillion level. But that absolute number is not what matters. As countries grow it is not abnormal for the debt of their governments to grow as well. What is of significance is that the absolute debt has not only been growing faster than GDP but has also recorded accelerated growth in the years since the Covid pandemic (see the trend in the index of debt volumes in Chart 1).

The year 2020 was extraordinary, as falling revenues and an unavoidable spike in expenditures induced by the pandemic widened the US Federal deficit and increased federal borrowing. But, as the pandemic waned, it was expected that this ‘unnatural’ spike would be reversed and debt levels would return to growing at or below the rate of growth of GDP.

That indeed seemed to be the case in 2021 and 2022 when the ratio of federal debt to GDP fell from its high 2020 level of 125.9 per cent to 119.6 and 118.4 per cent respectively. But that was still way above the pre-Covid level of 105.2 per cent, so the decline had some way to go. However, what occurred was a return to a faster increase in debt levels with the ratio of the federal debt-to-GDP rising to 121.5 per cent in 2025 (Chart 2).

As Chart 1 makes clear, two factors contributed to the renewed growth in the debt-to-GDP ratio. The first was an accelerated rise in the volume of debt itself. And the second, which partly accounts for the first, was a rise in the interest rate to levels not seen since the years immediately preceding the 2008 US-centred financial crisis. That rise in interest costs was in turn driven by the Federal Reserve’s policy response to the inflation that has persisted through the post-Covid years.

As is to be expected, a large deficit in the federal government’s budget necessitated the borrowing that drove the outstanding volume of federal debt. Even before the pandemic, the federal deficit had been rising from 2.4 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 4.6 per cent in 2019 (Chart 3). The explanation for that rise was an increase in borrowing costs from the near-zero level that prevailed between the last quarter of 2008 to the last quarter of 2015.

A steep reduction in interest rates to near zero was an important element in the toolkit used by the Federal Reserve to combat the Great Recession that followed the financial crisis. But by 2015 there were fears that this “unconventional” policy, as well as the policy of “quantitative easing” or bond purchases to inject liquidity into the system, could not continue.

That view was influenced by the evidence that the abundance of ‘cheap money’ had unleashed speculation in asset markets. Fears that the asset price bubble driven by that speculation could unravel with damaging consequences had convinced policy makers that it was time to unwind the regime of near-zero interest rates. Policy raised the 30-day Treasury rate from near zero to close to 2.5 per cent by late-2019, before Covid-impact fears and the actual pandemic took them back down to near zero for two years starting in the third quarter of 2020.

From early 2022, inflation reared its head and persisted, prodding the Fed to raise rates once again, stabilising the government’s borrowing costs at around 5 per cent. When Trump returned in 2025, he announced an ambitious agenda to reduce expenditures (through the exertions of the newly created Department of Government Efficiency headed initially by Elon Musk), and promised that he would reduce the deficit even while he offered business cronies significant direct tax benefits.

The promise of expenditure reduction through efficiency improvement yielded nothing however — expenditures actually increased (Chart 4). This was partly because ‘austerity’ notwithstanding, rising interest payments accounted for a growing share of current expenditures, neutralising the benefit of the limited expenditure cuts (Chart 5).

In the event, despite US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent’s declaration that he intends to reduce the federal deficit to 3 per cent of GDP, it remains at 6 per cent. But that is not the real challenge the government faces, which comes from other sources.

To start with, the Trump administration finds itself in an unusual fiscal bind — its debt is increasing partly because it is borrowing to cover rising interest payments on past debt.

Secondly, this occurs at a time when the costs of the war against Iran are exhausting its defence stockpiles necessitating massive spending increases. The administration had put in a supplemental appropriations request of $67.1 billion for the Department of Defence in June, which awaits Congress approval. But in July it managed to push through by a narrow 216-214 vote a $95 billion budget reconciliation package which reportedly includes $60 billion for defence. That too awaits final approval. So as opposed to $972 billion of funding for defence in financial year 2026 ending September, the request for national defence in FY2027 is placed at $1,154 billion. That would raise expenditures and widen the deficit, intensifying the debt-interest payment spiral.

Finally, with the Iran war and closure of the Strait of Hormuz keeping oil prices high, inflation in the US at around 3 per cent is above target and could rise further. Contrary to expectations, the signal from the new Federal Reserve Governor Kevin Warsh delivered at the Jackson Hole symposium in late August is that he is committed to the Fed’s 2 per cent inflation target and will rely on the interest rate as the main tool for inflation management. That possibly signals a policy rate hike, and definitely suggests that there are no plans for a rate cut given inflation. That would further widen the deficit and expand already bloated debt volumes.

The only way out for the administration to raise taxes and enhance tax revenues if it wants to reduce the deficit. But that is out of question for Trump, who is intent on appeasing big business and is already faced with an affordability crisis that precludes indirect tax increases. That leaves the US government mired in a debt trap of its own making.

Published on September 1, 2026

editorials.title: Sorting out seed exports
editorials.passage:
India has everything it needs to be one of the world’s leading seed suppliers, and is not yet one. That gap is worth examining, because very little of it has to do with science, capital or capability.

It is also not only an industry’s concern. Seed sits where farmer productivity, agricultural research, export competitiveness and foreign exchange earnings all meet. When this sector performs, farmers gain better genetics, value accumulates along the agricultural chain, and India claims a larger share of a global trade that is changing fast.

The raw material is there: the agro-climatic range to produce for both hemispheres, a research base of real depth, and growers who have been multiplying seed to export standard for decades. Demand too is not a constraint. Total seed exports grew from Rs 2,323 crore in 2024-25 to Rs 3,023 crore in 2025-26 - close to 30 per cent in a single year indicating that the world wants to buy Indian seed.

What that figure cannot tell us is whether our processes can keep pace. Even at that rate, India ships around $120 million of vegetable seed annually, ninth in the world, in a global trade of roughly $6 billion of which the Netherlands alone takes $2.4 billion. Our potential across all seed categories is put past $5 billion.

What keeps us short of it is rarely a policy decision. It is friction at the level of the individual transaction.

Picture a consignment of seed, contracted and paid for, sitting in a cold store while an export authorisation remains pending. For most products a delay of a few weeks is a commercial inconvenience. Seed is a living biological product tied to a narrow planting window. A delay can mean missing the season altogether, losing the commercial value of the consignment, and losing the customer to a competing origin.

Recent experience with restricted seed exports shows how this happens. Exporters have received deficiency letters at the export authorisation stage requiring that, where the germplasm is of Indian origin, their overseas buyer must first obtain approval from the National Biodiversity Authority. That condition does not appear in DGFT’s own Standard Operating Procedure, Trade Notice 26/2024-25 of December 2024, which the industry welcomed precisely because it established a legally enforceable affidavit mechanism for compliance with the Biological Diversity Act without holding up consignments.

Consider it from the buyer’s side.
