The Sangh mentality on women was recently exposed again in the right-wing hyperventilation over the actor Kriti Sanon after she appeared in a GIVA Raksha Bandhan ad wearing an Indo-Western outfit. The outfit promptly became a battlefield on which Hindutva warriors set out to “save” Indian civilisation. A shrill right-wing social-media uproar erupted as if Sanon’s clothing was a national moral emergency. BJP MP Kangana Ranaut demanded to know why anyone would tie a rakhi dressed in “a bikini or undergarments”. Faced with the outrage, the advertiser withdrew the ad. The ad was erased. What was also erased was the BJP-RSS’s so-called pretence at being pro-women. The attack on Sanon was a conservative witch-hunt dressed up as cultural concern. What offended the vigilantes was a woman’s freedom, a woman exercising free choice about her garments. How dare she be so free? Also Read: Nehru built parliamentary democracy. Modi has spent a decade dismantling it ‘ Empowerment’ with a male veto This episode followed a pattern. BJP big shots regularly police what women wear. In 2014, Manohar Lal Khattar said women should dress “decently” and inveighed against “short clothes” worn because of “Western influence”. In 2021, Tirath Singh Rawat blustered against women wearing “ ripped jeans ”. By the way, patriarchy does not operate only through men; it also recruits women to police other women. At the heart of the Sangh worldview is a simple refusal: women are not granted agency. At his recent women’s rally in Pune, Rahul Gandhi identified this trap. Women, he said , cannot be confined to the three identities of daughter, wife and mother. They belong first to themselves. His message was admirably unequivocal for a mainstream national leader: “Be loud. Be proud. Fight for your space in society. Smash the patriarchy.” The meaning of violence against women extends beyond physical assault. Denying a woman education, employment, property, mobility, political power or the right to speak is also violence. A cage does not become benign merely because its bars are decorated with flowers and ribbons. The BJP’s entire vocabulary for women runs through relationships with men. “Beti.” “Behan.” “Didi.” Women are judged by which man they are related to, not by what they say, think or write. For example, BJP trolls often respond to my writings by tagging my husband’s name. Why? What does my husband have to do with my work as a writer or in public life? Yet invariably the right wing counters my arguments by summoning a male relative, as if a woman’s words cannot be answered on their own. Patriarchy’s favourite woman is forever somebody’s something. A woman who claims independence, who exercises real choice, doesn’t fit anywhere in the Hindutva imagination. Last year, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar defended not sharing CCTV footage from polling booths for fear of violating the privacy of mothers, daughters, daughters-in-law and sisters. But privacy belongs to every voter. Why did Gyanesh Kumar reach specifically for the image of someone’s sister or mother? Why transform women exercising the public right to vote into sheltered female dependants whose modesty must be guarded? The BJP will point to Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao , Ujjwala cylinders and welfare transfers. A gas cylinder can ease a woman’s labour, but it cannot substitute for freedom. A party cannot declare itself emancipatory merely by dispensing daily benefits while continuing to police women’s clothes, love, speech and ambition. Empowerment is not something a benevolent male-dominated government hands down. Empowerment begins when the male veto is removed. A dangerous lakshman rekha The denial of personhood, individuality and freedom to women is the reason the BJP has never produced an Indira Gandhi or a Mamata Banerjee. Indira Gandhi and Mamata Banerjee were not merely women occupying high office, but women who authored their own political projects and took charge of their own destinies. Indira Gandhi was patronisingly dismissed as a goongi gudiya , a nasty slur. Yet she shattered that stereotype and emerged as a formidable political force. Mamata Banerjee built a political start-up from scratch, defeated the mighty 34-year-old Left Front (so-called “progressive” communists hurled dreadful misogynist abuse at her) and served three terms as chief minister, seven terms as MP and several times as Union minister. Indira Gandhi and Mamata Banerjee possessed, and possess, what BJP women lack and are denied — individual agency and autonomy. The freedom to pursue ambitions that are not defined and approved by men. The BJP can be vicious about independent high-achieving women. West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari’s recent threat against Mamata Banerjee, the erstwhile mentor under whom he rose, is an example. Adhikari recently declared that Mamata Banerjee should remain at home doing Facebook Lives, and said that he would “make arrangements” so she could never come out into the streets. Why? How does anyone in democratic India get the power to order anyone else to stay imprisoned at home? Would Suvendu Adhikari dare to tell a former three-term male chief minister to stay indoors and “take rest”? Adhikari unleashed patriarchy’s oldest, most venomous threat against Mamata Banerjee: order a woman to stay at home. The same double standard surfaced during the July 2026 student protests. In a video appealing for “forgiveness” for protesters who had used swear words against him, Narendra Modi described it as a “cultural shock” that “our daughters” were using such language. Why “our daughters”? Why not young citizens? When men speak harshly, the offence is treated as mere incivility. When a girl speaks her mind, her gender itself becomes an offence — a fall from prescribed notions of womanhood. The 15-year-old Modi referred to was attacked mercilessly. She and her widowed mother faced such savage online harassment that they were forced to leave their home. The message was unmistakable: cross the lakshman rekha and you, your face, your body, your family, home and entire future can all become targets. Your freedom exists on the patriarch’s permission and terms. Also Read: Don’t be so quick to write obituaries for the Opposition. We’re still alive and kicking The Sangh’s glass ceiling The denial of female autonomy is built into the Sangh’s institutional structure. RSS membership is entirely restricted to men. Women are directed into the parallel Rashtra Sevika Samiti. They can serve the same ideological project but can’t enter the organisation on equal institutional terms. What has befallen the BJP’s women leaders? The late Sushma Swaraj, her generation’s most eloquent parliamentarian, was sidelined. Swaraj was designated External Affairs minister, yet Modi personalised foreign policy around himself. Vasundhara Raje — arguably the closest the party has had to a genuine independent power centre, a two-time chief minister just as senior as Modi — has been kept at a distance by the Modi-Shah High Command. Former chief minister Uma Bharti, stereotyped as “unpredictable”, has also receded from the centre. None of them was ever allowed to step outside the box the BJP built for her, even when she had earned the right to. Smriti Irani is deployed primarily as a combatant against the Gandhis. Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta is a nominated face rather than a stalwart Delhi figure. Kangana Ranaut is known primarily for who she attacks. Nirmala Sitharaman, the finance minister, operates a ministry under the thumb of the PMO. Where does Sitharaman stand as an economic thinker? Is she a liberal, welfarist, free-marketeer or populist? She has never been permitted to articulate her own economic doctrine. “Modinomics” is spoken of, not “Sitharaman-nomics”. The BJP has not produced a single woman with independent standing and a public philosophy of her own — no one who has built a political movement from scratch the way Mamata Banerjee has, no one who commanded power and popularity the way Indira Gandhi did. Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath recently invoked the Manusmriti to attack Rahul Gandhi over his remarks on gender equality, but have women in UP been genuinely empowered? According to NCRB data, UP ranks first in crimes against women. Also Read: Don’t be so quick to write obituaries for the Opposition. We’re still alive and kicking A 21st-century misfit I have always argued that visibility is not equality and symbolism is not a power shift. This cynicism is clear in the Modi government’s approach to women’s reservation. Implementing the Women’s Reservation law passed in 2023 — providing for one-third representation of women in the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabhas — in the present 543-member Lok Sabha would mean a genuine redistribution of power. Women would get 181 seats, while 362 would go to men. Political parties would have to dislodge entrenched male incumbents and compel powerful men to cede actual space and share power. Yes, 181 women to 362 men is genuine power-sharing. But that is precisely what the Modi government has sought to avoid by linking women’s reservation with the delimitation exercise. This could dramatically expand the Lok Sabha, possibly to around 816 seats . In an 816-member House, one-third reservation would give women 273 seats while the remaining 543 would go to men. The absolute number of seats held by men would actually increase. Entrenched men would retain their places while women would be merely accommodated in the massively expanded House — 273 women and 543 men is by no means a fair distribution. It’s not a genuine transfer of power. It is the management of powerful men’s discomfort at the prospect of women entering Parliament in unprecedented numbers. As a columnist has written , it amounts to adding a “larger zenana wing to an enlarged patriarchal haveli” while leaving its male-dominated structure intact. Increase the size of the Ladies Compartment, but let the rest of the train remain with the men. This is not Nari Shakti . It is male appeasement dressed up as women’s empowerment. On a different but equally urgent note, a huge burden would be added on the taxpayer by increasing the number of MPs to over 800. The Sangh Parivar’s fixation with “love jihad” is another example of its entrenched patriarchy. It makes sense only if you assume women are incapable of making their own choices and are mere commodities to be protected from lustful Muslim men. The “love jihad” obsession infantilises women. Interestingly, the same voices demanding that Hindu women stay within the lines of “tradition” in their clothing are often the same as those insisting Muslim women cast off the traditional hijab. Actually, women’s clothing is never about women. It’s about who gets to decide what women can wear. The BJP-RSS’s patriarchy is cunningly disguised as “tradition” and “culture”. Instead, it is a violent woman-hating mindset intent on the denial of autonomy, individuality and freedom to women. Real freedom means recognising every woman’s right to wear a hijab, or remove it, choose a sari or ripped jeans or a bralette — and change her mind without seeking anyone’s ideological permission. Women’s bodies are not political territory. Women’s choices do not require cultural clearance from politicians, ministries, or social media troll armies. The BJP-RSS’s patriarchy is a misfit in the 21st century. Rahul Gandhi is spot on: this patriarchy needs to be smashed. Sagarika Ghose is a Rajya Sabha MP, All India Trinamool Congress. She tweets @sagarikaghose. Views are personal. (Edited by Asavari Singh)

Implementing the Women’s Reservation law passed in 2023 — providing for one-third representation of women in the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabhas — in the present 543-member Lok Sabha would mean a genuine redistribution of power. Women would get 181 seats, while 362 would go to men. Political parties would have to dislodge entrenched male incumbents and compel powerful men to cede actual space and share power. Yes, 181 women to 362 men is genuine power-sharing. But that is precisely what the Modi government has sought to avoid by linking women’s reservation with the delimitation exercise. This could dramatically expand the Lok Sabha, possibly to around 816 seats . In an 816-member House, one-third reservation would give women 273 seats while the remaining 543 would go to men. The absolute number of seats held by men would actually increase. Entrenched men would retain their places while women would be merely accommodated in the massively expanded House — 273 women and 543 men is by no means a fair distribution. It’s not a genuine transfer of power. It is the management of powerful men’s discomfort at the prospect of women entering Parliament in unprecedented numbers. As a columnist has written , it amounts to adding a “larger zenana wing to an enlarged patriarchal haveli” while leaving its male-dominated structure intact. Increase the size of the Ladies Compartment, but let the rest of the train remain with the men. This is not Nari Shakti . It is male appeasement dressed up as women’s empowerment. On a different but equally urgent note, a huge burden would be added on the taxpayer by increasing the number of MPs to over 800. The Sangh Parivar’s fixation with “love jihad” is another example of its entrenched patriarchy. It makes sense only if you assume women are incapable of making their own choices and are mere commodities to be protected from lustful Muslim men. The “love jihad” obsession infantilises women. Interestingly, the same voices demanding that Hindu women stay within the lines of “tradition” in their clothing are often the same as those insisting Muslim women cast off the traditional hijab. Actually, women’s clothing is never about women. It’s about who gets to decide what women can wear. The BJP-RSS’s patriarchy is cunningly disguised as “tradition” and “culture”. Instead, it is a violent woman-hating mindset intent on the denial of autonomy, individuality and freedom to women. Real freedom means recognising every woman’s right to wear a hijab, or remove it, choose a sari or ripped jeans or a bralette — and change her mind without seeking anyone’s ideological permission. Women’s bodies are not political territory. Women’s choices do not require cultural clearance from politicians, ministries, or social media troll armies. The BJP-RSS’s patriarchy is a misfit in the 21st century. Rahul Gandhi is spot on: this patriarchy needs to be smashed. Sagarika Ghose is a Rajya Sabha MP, All India Trinamool Congress. The attack on Sanon was a conservative witch-hunt dressed up as cultural concern. What offended the vigilantes was a woman’s freedom, a woman exercising free choice about her garments. How dare she be so free?

Also Read: Nehru built parliamentary democracy. Modi has spent a decade dismantling it ‘ Empowerment’ with a male veto This episode followed a pattern. BJP big shots regularly police what women wear. In 2014, Manohar Lal Khattar said women should dress “decently” and inveighed against “short clothes” worn because of “Western influence”. In 2021, Tirath Singh Rawat blustered against women wearing “ ripped jeans ”. By the way, patriarchy does not operate only through men; it also recruits women to police other women. At the heart of the Sangh worldview is a simple refusal: women are not granted agency. At his recent women’s rally in Pune, Rahul Gandhi identified this trap. Women, he said , cannot be confined to the three identities of daughter, wife and mother. They belong first to themselves. His message was admirably unequivocal for a mainstream national leader: “Be loud. Be proud. Fight for your space in society. Smash the patriarchy.” The meaning of violence against women extends beyond physical assault. Denying a woman education, employment, property, mobility, political power or the right to speak is also violence. A cage does not become benign merely because its bars are decorated with flowers and ribbons. The BJP’s entire vocabulary for women runs through relationships with men. “Beti.” “Behan.” “Didi.” Women are judged by which man they are related to, not by what they say, think or write. For example, BJP trolls often respond to my writings by tagging my husband’s name. Why? What does my husband have to do with my work as a writer or in public life? Yet invariably the right wing counters my arguments by summoning a male relative, as if a woman’s words cannot be answered on their own. Patriarchy’s favourite woman is forever somebody’s something. A woman who claims independence, who exercises real choice, doesn’t fit anywhere in the Hindutva imagination. Last year, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar defended not sharing CCTV footage from polling booths for fear of violating the privacy of mothers, daughters, daughters-in-law and sisters. But privacy belongs to every voter. Why did Gyanesh Kumar reach specifically for the image of someone’s sister or mother? Why transform women exercising the public right to vote into sheltered female dependants whose modesty must be guarded? The BJP will point to Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao , Ujjwala cylinders and welfare transfers. A gas cylinder can ease a woman’s labour, but it cannot substitute for freedom. A party cannot declare itself emancipatory merely by dispensing daily benefits while continuing to police women’s clothes, love, speech and ambition. Empowerment is not something a benevolent male-dominated government hands down. Empowerment begins when the male veto is removed. A dangerous lakshman rekha The denial of personhood, individuality and freedom to women is the reason the BJP has never produced an Indira Gandhi or a Mamata Banerjee. Indira Gandhi and Mamata Banerjee were not merely women occupying high office, but women who authored their own political projects and took charge of their own destinies. Indira Gandhi was patronisingly dismissed as a goongi gudiya , a nasty slur. Yet she shattered that stereotype and emerged as a formidable political force. Mamata Banerjee built a political start-up from scratch, defeated the mighty 34-year-old Left Front (so-called “progressive” communists hurled dreadful misogynist abuse at her) and served three terms as chief minister, seven terms as MP and several times as Union minister. Indira Gandhi and Mamata Banerjee possessed, and possess, what BJP women lack and are denied — individual agency and autonomy. The freedom to pursue ambitions that are not defined and approved by men. The BJP can be vicious about independent high-achieving women. West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari’s recent threat against Mamata Banerjee, the erstwhile mentor under whom he rose, is an example. Adhikari recently declared that Mamata Banerjee should remain at home doing Facebook Lives, and said that he would “make arrangements” so she could never come out into the streets. Why? How does anyone in democratic India get the power to order anyone else to stay imprisoned at home? Would Suvendu Adhikari dare to tell a former three-term male chief minister to stay indoors and “take rest”? Adhikari unleashed patriarchy’s oldest, most venomous threat against Mamata Banerjee: order a woman to stay at home. The same double standard surfaced during the July 2026 student protests. In a video appealing for “forgiveness” for protesters who had used swear words against him, Narendra Modi described it as a “cultural shock” that “our daughters” were using such language. Why “our daughters”? Why not young citizens? When men speak harshly, the offence is treated as mere incivility. When a girl speaks her mind, her gender itself becomes an offence — a fall from prescribed notions of womanhood. The 15-year-old Modi referred to was attacked mercilessly. She and her widowed mother faced such savage online harassment that they were forced to leave their home. The message was unmistakable: cross the lakshman rekha and you, your face, your body, your family, home and entire future can all become targets. At the heart of the Sangh worldview is a simple refusal: women are not granted agency. At his recent women’s rally in Pune, Rahul Gandhi identified this trap. Women, he said , cannot be confined to the three identities of daughter, wife and mother. They belong first to themselves. His message was admirably unequivocal for a mainstream national leader: “Be loud. Be proud. Fight for your space in society. Smash the patriarchy.”

The meaning of violence against women extends beyond physical assault. Denying a woman education, employment, property, mobility, political power or the right to speak is also violence. A cage does not become benign merely because its bars are decorated with flowers and ribbons. The BJP’s entire vocabulary for women runs through relationships with men. “Beti.” “Behan.” “Didi.” Women are judged by which man they are related to, not by what they say, think or write. For example, BJP trolls often respond to my writings by tagging my husband’s name. Why? What does my husband have to do with my work as a writer or in public life? Yet invariably the right wing counters my arguments by summoning a male relative, as if a woman’s words cannot be answered on their own. Patriarchy’s favourite woman is forever somebody’s something. A woman who claims independence, who exercises real choice, doesn’t fit anywhere in the Hindutva imagination. Last year, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar defended not sharing CCTV footage from polling booths for fear of violating the privacy of mothers, daughters, daughters-in-law and sisters. But privacy belongs to every voter. Why did Gyanesh Kumar reach specifically for the image of someone’s sister or mother? Why transform women exercising the public right to vote into sheltered female dependants whose modesty must be guarded? The BJP will point to Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao , Ujjwala cylinders and welfare transfers. A gas cylinder can ease a woman’s labour, but it cannot substitute for freedom. A party cannot declare itself emancipatory merely by dispensing daily benefits while continuing to police women’s clothes, love, speech and ambition. Empowerment is not something a benevolent male-dominated government hands down. Empowerment begins when the male veto is removed. A dangerous lakshman rekha The denial of personhood, individuality and freedom to women is the reason the BJP has never produced an Indira Gandhi or a Mamata Banerjee. Indira Gandhi and Mamata Banerjee were not merely women occupying high office, but women who authored their own political projects and took charge of their own destinies. Indira Gandhi was patronisingly dismissed as a goongi gudiya , a nasty slur. Yet she shattered that stereotype and emerged as a formidable political force. Mamata Banerjee built a political start-up from scratch, defeated the mighty 34-year-old Left Front (so-called “progressive” communists hurled dreadful misogynist abuse at her) and served three terms as chief minister, seven terms as MP and several times as Union minister. Adhikari recently declared that Mamata Banerjee should remain at home doing Facebook Lives, and said that he would “make arrangements” so she could never come out into the streets. Why? How does anyone in democratic India get the power to order anyone else to stay imprisoned at home? She and her widowed mother faced such savage online harassment that they were forced to leave their home. The message was unmistakable: cross the lakshman rekha and you, your face, your body, your family, home and entire future can all become targets. Vasundhara Raje — arguably the closest the party has had to a genuine independent power centre, a two-time chief minister just as senior as Modi — has been kept at a distance by the Modi-Shah High Command. Former chief minister Uma Bharti, stereotyped as “unpredictable”, has also receded from the centre. None of them was ever allowed to step outside the box the BJP built for her, even when she had earned the right to. Smriti Irani is deployed primarily as a combatant against the Gandhis. Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta is a nominated face rather than a stalwart Delhi figure. Kangana Ranaut is known primarily for who she attacks. Nirmala Sitharaman, the finance minister, operates a ministry under the thumb of the PMO. Where does Sitharaman stand as an economic thinker? Is she a liberal, welfarist, free-marketeer or populist? She has never been permitted to articulate her own economic doctrine. “Modinomics” is spoken of, not “Sitharaman-nomics”. The BJP has not produced a single woman with independent standing and a public philosophy of her own — no one who has built a political movement from scratch the way Mamata Banerjee has, no one who commanded power and popularity the way Indira Gandhi did. Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath recently invoked the Manusmriti to attack Rahul Gandhi over his remarks on gender equality, but have women in UP been genuinely empowered? According to NCRB data, UP ranks first in crimes against women. Also Read: Don’t be so quick to write obituaries for the Opposition. We’re still alive and kicking A 21st-century misfit I have always argued that visibility is not equality and symbolism is not a power shift. This cynicism is clear in the Modi government’s approach to women’s reservation. Implementing the Women’s Reservation law passed in 2023 — providing for one-third representation of women in the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabhas — in the present 543-member Lok Sabha would mean a genuine redistribution of power. Women would get 181 seats, while 362 would go to men. Political parties would have to dislodge entrenched male incumbents and compel powerful men to cede actual space and share power. Yes, 181 women to 362 men is genuine power-sharing. But that is precisely what the Modi government has sought to avoid by linking women’s reservation with the delimitation exercise. This could dramatically expand the Lok Sabha, possibly to around 816 seats . In an 816-member House, one-third reservation would give women 273 seats while the remaining 543 would go to men. The absolute number of seats held by men would actually increase. Entrenched men would retain their places while women would be merely accommodated in the massively expanded House — 273 women and 543 men is by no means a fair distribution. It’s not a genuine transfer of power. It is the management of powerful men’s discomfort at the prospect of women entering Parliament in unprecedented numbers. As a columnist has written , it amounts to adding a “larger zenana wing to an enlarged patriarchal haveli” while leaving its male-dominated structure intact. Increase the size of the Ladies Compartment, but let the rest of the train remain with the men. This is not Nari Shakti . It is male appeasement dressed up as women’s empowerment. On a different but equally urgent note, a huge burden would be added on the taxpayer by increasing the number of MPs to over 800. The Sangh Parivar’s fixation with “love jihad” is another example of its entrenched patriarchy. It makes sense only if you assume women are incapable of making their own choices and are mere commodities to be protected from lustful Muslim men. The “love jihad” obsession infantilises women. Interestingly, the same voices demanding that Hindu women stay within the lines of “tradition” in their clothing are often the same as those insisting Muslim women cast off the traditional hijab. Actually, women’s clothing is never about women. It’s about who gets to decide what women can wear. The BJP-RSS’s patriarchy is cunningly disguised as “tradition” and “culture”. Instead, it is a violent woman-hating mindset intent on the denial of autonomy, individuality and freedom to women. Real freedom means recognising every woman’s right to wear a hijab, or remove it, choose a sari or ripped jeans or a bralette — and change her mind without seeking anyone’s ideological permission. Women’s bodies are not political territory. Women’s choices do not require cultural clearance from politicians, ministries, or social media troll armies. The BJP-RSS’s patriarchy is a misfit in the 21st century. Rahul Gandhi is spot on: this patriarchy needs to be smashed. Sagarika Ghose is a Rajya Sabha MP, All India Trinamool Congress. She tweets @sagarikaghose. Views are personal. (Edited by Asavari Singh)

editorials.title: Gurugram is a city of private enclaves connected by public failure
editorials.passage:
I f Gur ugram could manifest as an emotion over the last week, it would probably choose rage and helplessness. In the city that houses the offices of more than half the world’s Fortune 500 companies, an exhausted little schoolgirl sat on the highest bench of a daily needs shop, surrounded by a pool of murky water, and wailed into the open. Adults stuck at the shop tried to console her, but the child—holding on to her pink plastic water bottle with all her might—would not stop crying for her parents. Two other equally morose children sat in front of her, stranded after their school bus gave way after the city experienced 75 mm rainfall in the span of a workday. These kids weren’t the only ones stuck in the deluge . About a dozen private-school buses carrying kids from nursery upward were mired nose to tail in the filthy pond that sprang up between Subhash Chowk and Rail Vihar. One hopes that the children reached home safely, though the trauma they endured will likely linger. T heir parents suffer with them. Siddharth Kasid, 39, all but gave up on Gurugram that day, after witnessing firsthand the danger that his child was in. The employee of a multinational investment bank spent the afternoon looking at his five-year-old daughter’s location on an app, tracking the school bus’s movement. When Kasid realised that the flooded stretch outside his home meant that the bus wouldn’t be able to reach it, he started walking toward it through waist-deep water, dodging open manholes and rubble from the m etro construction—a walk he later described as “more intense and gruelling than the trek to Vaishno Devi”.

The employee of a multinational investment bank spent the afternoon looking at his five-year-old daughter’s location on an app, tracking the school bus’s movement. When Kasid realised that the flooded stretch outside his home meant that the bus wouldn’t be able to reach it, he started walking toward it through waist-deep water, dodging open manholes and rubble from the m etro construction—a walk he later described as “more intense and gruelling than the trek to Vaishno Devi”.

On reaching the spot, Kasid found 10 stalled buses with very young children inside. Along with his daughter—who asked if it was Holi—he was able to bring back a few other students with him, walking them single-file. Kasid then echoed the question several of Gurugram’s residents , rich and poor , have been asking for years. “We pay hefty taxes and exorbitant school fees, and this is how the city is maintained? I hate it now,” he said. “Gurugram is simply not worth living in anymore.” By next afternoon, a portal opened up on a stretch of the service lane at IFFCO Chowk and swallowed Gurugram’s pretensions about itself. Underneath the crucial junction, which connects the city with the international airport and South Delhi, is a master sewer line bearing the waste of DLF Phase II and MG Road. The line had been leaking for a while, and last week, it finally dissolved the earth holding up the carriageway and turned into a sinkhole. This isn’t even novel for IFFCO Chowk: The ground has opened up in 2019, 2020, and 2021, when part of a retaining wall of a flyover collapsed. Of course, now 20 metres of the pipe will be replaced, another 100 relined. The Gurugram Metropolitan Development Authority ( GMDA ) has also—post-haste—floated a Rs 8 crore tender to upgrade the master sewer on other stretches. A sinking feeling Gurugram’s residents no longer register the city’s monsoon as a surprise. They experience it as paranoia, anticipating the rains with dread. After all, this is a city of private enclaves connected with one another by public failure. Last week, the GMDA’s master drain backed up into South City II once again. Two years prior, the same waterlogging had caused the death of a pet dog, who got electrocuted. South City II’s residents were forced to switch on their own pumps to push the sewage runoff back onto the public road. For their attempts to save their houses, which cost upwards of Rs 3 crore, the residents were threatened with an FIR for damaging public property. For three decades since the city’s inception, Gurugram’s citizens have made their peace with paying double for the services their taxes should uphold. The private economy thrives when the city’s richest become convinced that they can buy their way out of a terrible state of affairs. Water—drawn from a dwindling water table—arrives by private tankers, priced anywhere between Rs 8,400 and Rs 26,000 in the peak summer months. Electricity is from 24-hour power backup, advertised on brochures of real-estate companies. Kids will anyway go to private schools, as their parents did . Private security is uniformed and ready with their boom barriers and registers. The city authorities will provide waste management when they feel like it—otherwise, RWAs will step up to fill in the gaps. Every essential service can be ordered off an app, and the options are aplenty. I’m actually surprised that Gurugram’s entrepreneurial spirit hasn’t yet managed to convince the authorities that they should be allowed to operate private sewer lines or stormwater drains. And if that works, can private stretches of the highway be far behind? (Though the Delhi-Gurugram Expressway was built and tolled under a private concession, which the NHAI eventually took back in 2014.) Alas, these services remain stubbornly, inconveniently public, treating the 100-crore apartment and the tin shanty with the same measure of complete indifference. There are limits to secession, but at least in this one aspect, the rich and the poor are equal losers. Also read: There is no fundamental right to cheap Kumbh airfares The ‘flexible planning’ of Gurugram Last week, the Indian Express reported that in a briefing to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Haryana chief minister Nayab Singh Saini put forth two modish-sounding proposals to tackle Gurugram’s perennial waterlogging issue, as part of a larger overhaul of the city’s drainage network. These include specialised injection wells—a subsurface structure that channels rainwater into aquifers—with an absorption capacity of 48-80 litres per second. It works in conjunction with high-volume underground storage tanks, meant to capture surface runoff immediately. All of this will be monitored via a SCADA system, the standard among critical infrastructure industries. All these solutions—due to be implemented over a one-year timeline for four major bottlenecks—are straight out of the technocratic imagination. High-impact projects meant for high-velocity metropolises populated by a driven, high-intent population. Later on, the same report cited a planning expert trying his best to sound optimistic about the proposals. CR Bisnoi, retired Executive Engineer of the Municipal Corporation of Gurugram, said that “what Gurugram needs are also some old-school solutions—making ponds and reservoirs in parks, and removing encroachments from drains.” The water bodies Bisnoi is referring to have dwindled in the last few decades. In 1956, Gurugram had more than 640 natural water bodies; by 2018, that number stood at 251. These are the results when a city is cobbled together through the statutory power of relaxation, which allowed the Haryana government to waive land-use restrictions in the public interest. Anthropologist Shubhra Gururani, who has studied Gurugram closely, posits the concept of “flexible planning”. “The making of Gurgaon relies on regulated improvisations of urban land laws that pave the way for political/caste elites to productively navigate the ambiguities in the plan, reconcile multiple contradictions, and enlist a range of material and symbolic techniques to produce an uneven geography of urbanization,” she wrote in the introduction to Subaltern Frontiers of Agrarian Urbanism (2023). For a city assembled by private builders, there were few pesky regulations to adhere to. Between July 2025 and March 2026, the state issued 1,500 occupancy certificates prematurely. When 22 housing societies were inspected , 14 were found to be only concrete shells. Nowhere is this attitude more apparent than in the fact that Gurugram elected its first municipal mayor in 2011, in an election riddled with allegations of horse-trading. For context, the MGF Metropolitan Mall opened its doors in 1998. Also read: Mohan Bhagwat doesn’t decide if Muslims belong in India. The Constitution does A case of two laados Public services improve when people with the power to become a nuisance to the government insist that they improve. A few days ago, 14,000 contractual sanitation and fire department workers struck work for three weeks, and piles of garbage arose again in Gurugram. Several RWAs were forced to ask the state to hand them the municipal sanitation budget so they could hire private contractors themselves. Gurugram’s residents are no doubt responding to a crisis the best way they know how. But the trouble with private arrangements is that it slowly erodes the collective bargaining power of a constituency. And that’s why Gurugram MLA Mukesh Sharma’s Instagram feed is pristine: It is full of inaugurations and meetings he has addressed. There isn’t a single post acknowledging the distress that the city’s residents have endured. CM Saini, meanwhile, is busy campaigning in Punjab, congratulating the p rime m inister, blaming the Congress, but hasn’t yet been able to reassure the beleaguered citizens of his state. He did post a very sweet, heartwarming message for a young child from Northeast India, who had spoken about being labelled “Chinese” in a viral video. “You’re a daughter of India, laado !” Saini comforted her. She no doubt is—but so is the young girl in that other viral video clutching her pink bottle, who also happens to be a daughter of Haryana. Maybe someday, that video will also make its way to Gurugram’s representatives. Karanjeet Kaur is a journalist, former editor of Arré, and a partner at TWO Design. She tweets @Kaju_Katri. Views are personal. (Edited by Prasanna Bachchhav)

editorials.title: The CNG hike nobody questioned is hiding India’s most expensive untold secret
editorials.passage:
​ O n the morning of 29 August, Indraprastha Gas Limited increased the price of CNG in Delhi by Rs 3.89 per kilogram. This marks the fifth increase this year. While this adjustment may appear to be just another incremental rise in fuel costs and commuting expenses, it calls for a deeper examination. The CNG hike is part of a broader government strategy that has unfolded over the past seven months in the wake of the fuel crisis. Primary government data shows how prices were raised selectively, giving insight into governmental priorities and decision-making processes. Also Read: India’s housing market isn’t cooling down, it’s repositioning for what comes next

While this adjustment may appear to be just another incremental rise in fuel costs and commuting expenses, it calls for a deeper examination.

The CNG hike is part of a broader government strategy that has unfolded over the past seven months in the wake of the fuel crisis. Primary government data shows how prices were raised selectively, giving insight into governmental priorities and decision-making processes. Also Read: India’s housing market isn’t cooling down, it’s repositioning for what comes next

The CNG hike is part of a broader government strategy that has unfolded over the past seven months in the wake of the fuel crisis. Primary government data shows how prices were raised selectively, giving insight into governmental priorities and decision-making processes.

Also Read: India’s housing market isn’t cooling down, it’s repositioning for what comes next

The shock that started it The narrative originates in West Asia rather than Delhi. The Indian Basket crude oil price, which serves as the benchmark for India’s actual expenditure on imported crude, remained stable between $63 and $69 per barrel during January and February 2026. However, within a single month, it surged by 64 per cent to $113, coinciding with the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz due to renewed regional conflict. The price reached a peak of nearly $114 in April, decreased through June and July as tensions subsided, and began to rise again by August, coinciding with the fifth increase in Delhi’s CNG bill. A war abroad, an oil shock and a subsequent domestic price increase is a familiar narrative. Such events, in isolation, might not necessarily require extensive analysis. What matters, however, is India’s response to this shock — the transmission of its effects was neither uniform nor transparent in its magnitude. A textbook case of price discrimination, run on gas cylinders In economics, the practice of charging different prices to different buyers or groups of buyers for the same product is known as price discrimination. This concept was formalised by economist AC Pigou in the 1920s to describe such segmented pricing strategies. During the crisis, India implemented a form of price discrimination without explicitly labelling it as such. In Delhi, the price of household LPG cylinders increased by only 10 per cent over the entire period, from Rs 853 to Rs 942, in two calibrated increments. In contrast, the price of commercial cylinders, which are essential for restaurants, hotels, and small businesses, increased by 79 per cent during the same timeframe, from Rs 1,740 to Rs 3,114, before decreasing slightly as global prices stabilised. According to Pigou, price discrimination requires a seller possessing both pricing power and the capability to differentiate between buyers. India’s oil marketing companies exhibit these characteristics, and the disparity they established between household and commercial pricing persisted beyond its inception, subsequently impacting their balance sheets. The LPG under-recoveries, defined as the discrepancy between the actual cost of fuel and its selling price, were estimated by Crisil to have reached approximately Rs 22,000 crore by May and exceeded Rs 59,000 crore by the end of July. The government’s confirmed figure, presented to Parliament, indicated that total under-recoveries across all sensitive fuels amounted to Rs 2.19 lakh crore for the quarter. This scenario illustrates a secondary, less conspicuous concept known as fiscal illusion. This phenomenon involves a genuine cost that does not manifest as government expenditure during the period it is incurred, as it is borne by a state company rather than being recorded in the Budget. Consequently, the household consumer perceives stability, while the exchequer remains unaffected temporarily. The financial obligation exists but remains obscured from the public, who ultimately bear the cost, until it necessitates recapitalisation, a price adjustment, or an unanticipated subsidy. Prices that move like a calendar, not a market Petrol and diesel introduce another dimension to the story: the mechanism by which prices were adjusted. In a textbook competitive market, prices are expected to adjust continuously in response to cost fluctuations. However, the petrol price in Delhi remained fixed at Rs 94.77 for four months. It then increased on four occasions over a ten-day period in May, reaching Rs 102.12, and has remained unchanged for three months despite fluctuations in global oil prices. Diesel followed the same pattern within the same ten-day period, increasing by 8.6 per cent to Rs 95.20. Two fuels, sold by the same state retailer, were repriced in lockstep during one narrow window and then held flat regardless of what the underlying commodity did afterward. This is not a market price finding its level. It is an administered price, set periodically by decision rather than continuously by markets, much like regulated utility prices — except without the same public rate-setting process utilities are typically subject to. Diesel alone is understood to have carried the largest share of that quarter’s under-recovery burden of any single fuel. This is unsurprising for the fuel that moves freight and buses, and feeds into the cost of transporting nearly everything else in the country. The real issue is transparency Now, none of this makes the underlying decision indefensible. It is reasonable for a government to shield households from a global cost shock, especially when a war disrupts a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply. Most governments facing similar shocks adopt comparable measures. A century ago, economist Frank Knight distinguished between risk, which can be priced and insured against, and uncertainty, whose scale and duration are unknown. A war of uncertain length exemplifies uncertainty in Knight’s terms, and a government’s effort to cushion its citizens against it is not unreasonable. What is avoidable, however, is the lack of transparency. A subsidy that appears in a budget line undergoes scrutiny, parliamentary debate, and eventual reform if it becomes unjustifiable. In contrast, a subsidy that appears as a quietly increasing under-recovery on a state company’s books lacks such scrutiny until the figure becomes too significant to ignore. At that point, the necessary correction is often more severe than it would have been had the true cost been apparent from the outset. Also Read: RBI’s nine-day U-turn is a masterclass in how not to talk to markets What honesty would actually look like The resolution does not require reversing the decision to prioritise household protection. The cost of that decision simply needs to be made visible while it is still being incurred, rather than months later through a parliamentary statement or a ratings agency estimate. The Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) already publishes retail prices daily, as shown in Figures 1 and 3. A similar approach could apply to Oil Marketing Companies’ (OMCs) under-recovery figures on a consistent monthly basis, rather than through sporadic disclosures contingent on ministerial discretion. Any prolonged price freeze, such as the current stabilisation of petrol and diesel prices since May, could also be accompanied by the publication of the shadow price it would reflect if aligned with the international benchmark. This would make the extent of the discrepancy visible in real time rather than reconstructed retrospectively from archived data. In addition, diesel, given its disproportionate impact on fiscal costs, requires its own distinct reporting line rather than being subsumed into a combined petrol-diesel-LPG figure. A government that shields its citizens from a conflict it did not initiate has made a defensible decision. However, a government that allows its citizens to comprehend the actual magnitude of what they are being shielded from has made a more robust decision. Currently, the only method to ascertain the true cost of this crisis is to independently reconstruct the data, fuel by fuel, from PPAC’s archives, as was necessary for the three figures in this analysis. A figure that requires manual reconstruction seems to be one that the public was never intended to perceive clearly from the outset. Bidisha Bhattacharya is ThePrint Consulting Editor (Economics) and an Associate Fellow, Chintan Research Foundation. She tweets @Bidishabh. Views are personal. (Edited by Asavari Singh)

This would make the extent of the discrepancy visible in real time rather than reconstructed retrospectively from archived data. In addition, diesel, given its disproportionate impact on fiscal costs, requires its own distinct reporting line rather than being subsumed into a combined petrol-diesel-LPG figure. A government that shields its citizens from a conflict it did not initiate has made a defensible decision. However, a government that allows its citizens to comprehend the actual magnitude of what they are being shielded from has made a more robust decision. Currently, the only method to ascertain the true cost of this crisis is to independently reconstruct the data, fuel by fuel, from PPAC’s archives, as was necessary for the three figures in this analysis. A figure that requires manual reconstruction seems to be one that the public was never intended to perceive clearly from the outset. During the crisis, India implemented a form of price discrimination without explicitly labelling it as such.

In Delhi, the price of household LPG cylinders increased by only 10 per cent over the entire period, from Rs 853 to Rs 942, in two calibrated increments. In contrast, the price of commercial cylinders, which are essential for restaurants, hotels, and small businesses, increased by 79 per cent during the same timeframe, from Rs 1,740 to Rs 3,114, before decreasing slightly as global prices stabilised. According to Pigou, price discrimination requires a seller possessing both pricing power and the capability to differentiate between buyers. India’s oil marketing companies exhibit these characteristics, and the disparity they established between household and commercial pricing persisted beyond its inception, subsequently impacting their balance sheets. The LPG under-recoveries, defined as the discrepancy between the actual cost of fuel and its selling price, were estimated by Crisil to have reached approximately Rs 22,000 crore by May and exceeded Rs 59,000 crore by the end of July. The government’s confirmed figure, presented to Parliament, indicated that total under-recoveries across all sensitive fuels amounted to Rs 2.19 lakh crore for the quarter. This scenario illustrates a secondary, less conspicuous concept known as fiscal illusion. This phenomenon involves a genuine cost that does not manifest as government expenditure during the period it is incurred, as it is borne by a state company rather than being recorded in the Budget. Consequently, the household consumer perceives stability, while the exchequer remains unaffected temporarily. The financial obligation exists but remains obscured from the public, who ultimately bear the cost, until it necessitates recapitalisation, a price adjustment, or an unanticipated subsidy. Prices that move like a calendar, not a market Petrol and diesel introduce another dimension to the story: the mechanism by which prices were adjusted. In a textbook competitive market, prices are expected to adjust continuously in response to cost fluctuations. However, the petrol price in Delhi remained fixed at Rs 94.77 for four months. It then increased on four occasions over a ten-day period in May, reaching Rs 102.12, and has remained unchanged for three months despite fluctuations in global oil prices. Diesel followed the same pattern within the same ten-day period, increasing by 8.6 per cent to Rs 95.20. Two fuels, sold by the same state retailer, were repriced in lockstep during one narrow window and then held flat regardless of what the underlying commodity did afterward. This is not a market price finding its level. It is an administered price, set periodically by decision rather than continuously by markets, much like regulated utility prices — except without the same public rate-setting process utilities are typically subject to. Diesel alone is understood to have carried the largest share of that quarter’s under-recovery burden of any single fuel. This is unsurprising for the fuel that moves freight and buses, and feeds into the cost of transporting nearly everything else in the country. The real issue is transparency Now, none of this makes the underlying decision indefensible. It is reasonable for a government to shield households from a global cost shock, especially when a war disrupts a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply. Most governments facing similar shocks adopt comparable measures. A century ago, economist Frank Knight distinguished between risk, which can be priced and insured against, and uncertainty, whose scale and duration are unknown. In contrast, a subsidy that appears as a quietly increasing under-recovery on a state company’s books lacks such scrutiny until the figure becomes too significant to ignore. At that point, the necessary correction is often more severe than it would have been had the true cost been apparent from the outset. editorials.title: What Grand Mufti Kanthapuram needs to know about Islam before ordering Muslim women inside
editorials.passage:
A t the Hubbu Rasool Conference in Kochi, India’s Grand Mufti Kanthapuram AP Aboobacker Musliyar from Keralam compared Muslim women to a gold necklace that must be locked safely inside a box so it does not lose its shine or value. He warned that women who step into the public sphere invite “great destruction.” The Quran, he declared, requires them to remain confined to their homes. He is wrong. Not offensive-wrong. Theologically wrong. And as a Muslim woman who prays, fasts, and reads her own Quran instead of waiting for a man to read it to her, I want to explain exactly why.

A t the Hubbu Rasool Conference in Kochi, India’s Grand Mufti Kanthapuram AP Aboobacker Musliyar from Keralam compared Muslim women to a gold necklace that must be locked safely inside a box so it does not lose its shine or value. He warned that women who step into the public sphere invite “great destruction.” The Quran, he declared, requires them to remain confined to their homes.

He is wrong. Not offensive-wrong. Theologically wrong. And as a Muslim woman who prays, fasts, and reads her own Quran instead of waiting for a man to read it to her, I want to explain exactly why.

He is wrong. Not offensive-wrong. Theologically wrong.

And as a Muslim woman who prays, fasts, and reads her own Quran instead of waiting for a man to read it to her, I want to explain exactly why.

Islam’s first convert wasn’t a man. It was Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, a wealthy, independent businesswoman who ran her own trading caravans across Arabia. She employed the Prophet, Muhammad, judged his character and reputation, and then proposed him for marriage herself. This is recorded across the earliest biographical sources on the Prophet’s life known as Seerah. However, there is no recorded account of the Prophet commanding Khadijah or even requesting her to abandon public economic life. Khadijah wasn’t hidden away. If female public presence did cause “great destruction,” Islam’s very first supporter would have been a walking contradiction of her own faith. Then there is Aisha, the daughter of the first caliph, Abu Bakr, and the Prophet’s wife. Known as a prolific scholar, she narrated over 2,000 hadith — recorded reports of the Prophet’s sayings and actions — playing a signficant role in preserving his teachings and contributing to Islamic law and scholarship. Even male companions and later scholars came to her for knowledge of fiqh (deep understanding of Islamic laws), medicine, poetry, and the Prophet’s life. They actively sought her out on these matters, and she corrected and taught them. A prominent companion of Prophet Muhammad, Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari famously said: “Never was a hadith unclear to us, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, and we asked Aisha about it except that we found knowledge concerning it with her.” Historians count around 88 scholars, men included, who studied directly under her. Apart from scholarly knowledge, women also accompanied armies to carry water, treat the wounded, and provide nursing support, while some also took up weapons when circumstances demanded it. A well-known example is Nusaybah bint Ka‘b , who fought at the Battle of Uhud and defended Prophet Muhammad when the Muslim lines broke. None of these are mere historical claims; they are the bedrock of Sunni hadith literature that clerics like Kanthapuram claim to represent. Centuries later, a woman named Fatima al-Fihri inherited her father’s fortune in Fez, Morocco, and used it to establish a mosque in 859 CE, which eventually became an educational centre. Today, the University of al-Qarawiyyin is recognised by UNESCO and the Guinness World Records as the oldest continuously operating, degree-granting university on Earth, older than Oxford (UK) and Bologna (Italy). A Muslim woman founded higher education as we know it. Centuries before Europe even had it. Also read: ‘Ghazwa-e-Hind’ didn’t come from Islamic scholarship. It came from modern politics Muslim women in public sphere Kanthapuram invoked “the Holy Quran” as his source. But as the examples above show, women were never written out of public life in the Quran. The real requirement was modesty, not only for women, but for men too. Surah An-Nur, verse 24:30 tells believing men to lower their gaze and guard their chastity first, before women are even addressed. Only in the next verse, 24:31, are believing women given the same instruction, with additional guidance on covering. Hadith also lay down clear standards of modesty for men — from what they should cover to warnings against silk, gold, and pompous display. So, modesty in Islam was never a woman-only rule; it applies to men’s bodies and behaviour too. However, nowhere in this passage, or anywhere else in the Quran, does it say women must be barred from public life. Today, across the Muslim world, women continue to refute such claims. Indonesia, the largest Muslim-majority country, has had a woman president, Megawati Sukarnoputri. Singapore has also seen Halimah Yacob, a practicing muslim woman, serve as president for six years. Western countries, like the United States, are still waiting for one. Malaysia has also had Wan Azizah Wan Ismail serve as Deputy Prime Minister. Women teach in seminaries, issue fatwas , and serve as judges and parliamentarians in many Muslim societies. Their existence alone dismantles the claim that public visibility or positions of leadership are somehow un-Islamic. Some of the women occupy the same seat that conservative Muslim scholars assume only they can occupy. Ingrid Mattson was the first woman to head the Islamic Society of North America. Scholars such as Dr Zainab Alwani, Dr Farhat Ishtiyaq, and Yasmin Mogahed are part of a growing, global body of Muslim women doing serious theological work; not asking permission to exist in public, but producing the scholarship itself. Yet, the idea that Muslim women belong only in the private sphere keeps resurfacing in its most extreme form in the modern world. The Taliban’s extreme restrictions, such as banning girls from secondary education, silencing women’s voices in public, or confining them almost entirely to the private sphere, are often presented as pure Islam. But they are not. They mix rigid, controversial interpretations of certain texts with deep-rooted Pashtun tribal codes of honour and control. Many Muslim scholars and communities worldwide reject this model when discussing the broader vision of Islam. Honour and dignity are not maintained by locking women away. They are preserved through knowledge and mutual respect. The Prophet elevated the status of women in a society that buried daughters alive. That legacy cannot be honoured by pushing women back into the shadows. (Edited by Prashant Dixit)

Scholars such as Dr Zainab Alwani, Dr Farhat Ishtiyaq, and Yasmin Mogahed are part of a growing, global body of Muslim women doing serious theological work; not asking permission to exist in public, but producing the scholarship itself. Yet, the idea that Muslim women belong only in the private sphere keeps resurfacing in its most extreme form in the modern world. The Taliban’s extreme restrictions, such as banning girls from secondary education, silencing women’s voices in public, or confining them almost entirely to the private sphere, are often presented as pure Islam. But they are not. They mix rigid, controversial interpretations of certain texts with deep-rooted Pashtun tribal codes of honour and control. Many Muslim scholars and communities worldwide reject this model when discussing the broader vision of Islam. Honour and dignity are not maintained by locking women away. They are preserved through knowledge and mutual respect. The Prophet elevated the status of women in a society that buried daughters alive.
