editorials.title: Is the sword central to the Hindutva aesthetic? A new book looks for answers
editorials.passage:
On October 3, 2022, the News Minute reported that 200 people belonging to different faiths marched in Udupi in Karnataka to mark the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi. A much bigger rally of around 10,000 people came in response, brandishing swords and chanting slogans in support of the Hindu rashtra. Swords are out on various such occasions. Swords are out as there are actual wars to fight outside. All over India, festivals such as Dussehra and Ram Navami are turning into sword rallies. From Ranchi and Hazaribagh in Jharkhand to Gulbarga in Karnataka, from Haldia in West Bengal to Nalanda in Bihar, people are marching with swords. The sword is turning into an object of worship. A sacrificial object and a celebratory artefact.

Having swords is a matter of pride. More than anything else, the sword is about social status. It is about being a Kshatriya. It is about claiming the Kshatriya impunity. Of course, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh are the laboratories of Hindutva, where its activists openly distribute swords. Their swords come out for any occasion. Just as some ride a bulldozer in their wedding procession, others cut a birthday cake with a sword. The weapons are also used for various other occasions. To celebrate birthdays, at weddings, in death and to take oaths and to welcome guests. Reports say that as the cities were preparing for Ram Navami celebrations, the devotees were busy buying swords.

But why swords, I wonder. Why do Hindutva followers have to display swords when they can display shotguns? They could have exhibited an AK-47 or an INSAS in marches and processions. The weapons could have better matched their sense of superiority. One expected that Hindutva would brandish some automatic guns – if not the real, then replicas, maybe toy guns or air pistols. The arms could have matched the modern age, instead of the medieval age. They should not have any problem exhibiting them, as they have access to power and impunity. They have the right to display anything they like: muscles, weapons, hatred and fear. Why do their heroes still ride horses when they could have warplanes, the Rafale jets?

But why a sword, a horse, a turban, a moustache? What do these symbols relate to? The associations prompt me to ask a plain question: Does a cultural artefact have a caste?

The sword has no place in modern warfare. Writes Damon Young in “Why Are Swords Still a Thing?”: “We live in an age of anti-aircraft lasers, electromagnetic railguns, and rifle sights with ballistic computers. American drone pilots in New Mexico kill children more than 11,000 kilometres away, in Afghanistan. Swords have almost no place on the modern battlefield – even bayonets are becoming rare.” Swords have gone obsolete in combat. But they keep appearing. Leaders who travel by high-tech planes and use cutting-edge technology in their everyday lives wield swords at public rallies. Men who run big tech companies in Silicon Valley carry swords at their weddings. Is the idea of swords in the time of shotguns an anachronism? What significance do the archaic medieval objects hold in our present, in a specific sociocultural context? And in relation to Hindutva?

If the upper castes are buying swords to celebrate their heritage and past, the so-called lower castes also show a desire to display them to claim their participation in the present. It shows that a sword is about power and possession. It is about succession, about domination. One who could not buy a sword uses a stick and wields it like a sword to look and feel like a Kshatriya. Swords are making a comeback because of their heritage quality. It is about past glory and prestige. Also, in contrast, the resurgence of the weapon is less about the past and more about the present. Nayanjot Lahiri points out: “The history of the use of metals in the Indian archaeological record is much more than a catalogue of artefact types and their technological make-up: it also denotes a cultural situation which seems to be very specifically Indian.”

What does a sword symbolise in our present time? Why does Hindutva want to bring it back? The relationship of the sword and Hindutva is reciprocal. Hence, we should ask what Hindutva does with the archaic object and value, and what swords give to Hindutva in return. Swords have always been around, but their overwhelming presence is new; the symbolism existed, but the context is new. It is out in exhibitions and processions, in marches and war cries. It is part of the glorious past that Hindutva wants to invoke, but it also exists in performative utterances, like Hindu khatre mein hai (Hindus are in danger).

When the tongue comes as a two-edged sword: “If I were born during the Tipu regime, […] I would be known as someone who raised his sword against a communal person,” said CT Ravi, a BJP leader. The narrative accompanying swords has always come with exaggeration. Maharana Pratap’s sword was supposed to weigh more than 200 kg and be bigger than his kingdom. The media are producing weaponised talk, where the reference to a sword is rhetorical. But we have also seen how anchors are appearing with swords and war costumes in the newsroom. The distinction between the rhetorical and the real and the word and the body disappears. The sharp-edged weapon not only denotes power through its physicality, but it also projects sharp hatred with its edge. It is a somatic weapon; it is psychological. It is historical and archaeological; it is also a social weapon. If the sword of the past had a clear varna-caste intent with its Kshatriya values and Dalits and Shudras as its target, a sword in our time has a clear anti-Muslim intent.

A sword is a weapon that is more than a weapon. Call it a pure weapon or an artefact, an emblem of power or an object of pride, its presence has been massively felt with the rise of Hindutva. Though one can see it as a mere coincidence, the association of Hindutva and the sword does not seem to be a chance one. It is not surprising that we are seeing more swords than we have ever seen in the near past. Its presence is overpowering, from weddings to festivals, from rallies to ceremonies, in epics, metaphors, memorials and processions.

We are witnessing an overriding presence of the sword. It already has its residual presence in a caste–feudal society. Grooms still walk with swords as if they are not going to a wedding but a battle, not to marry but to murder the bride. It is not surprising that the sword has been a highly visible part of the jhankis (tableaux) and shaadis (weddings). It decorates the memorials of heroes, leaders and martyrs. It commemorates the histories and genealogies of privileged communities in galleries. It appears proudly in museums, in epic dramas on screen and in public displays off screen. It walks naked in the democratic public sphere, diving deep into the digital world. It marches in rallies, in crowds in the hands of lynching mobs. It dances naked, robed in power, and threatening democracy. It has come with a new function and a new fascination. It is a new fetish. It’s the new fashion. Hey, let’s walk with swords.

Taking a leaf from Ambedkar, we can read the resurgence of swords as the coming of Kshatriya values. It is a weapon of counter-revolution. This is not only a counter-revolution against the rise of the oppressed but also to make a new cut. If Hindutva is getting subalternised, as some scholars would argue, why not bring more subaltern symbols, such as plough, sickle or spade (if it is just a matter of cutting). Strong Kshatriya ideals have been the core discussion of Hindutva ideologues. They want to rescue the Kshatriyas from their medieval humiliations and reignite their power. They have to rescue Kshatriyas from the baggage of the medieval age to carry on the Hindutva agenda. But why a sword? The sword is about symbolic power. What else? It is about a tacit and unconscious mode of cultural domination. It is not so much about its value as a cutting weapon; it is about its cult value – how much fetish it can create. It is a cult weapon. Its power lies in its aura and oration. A sword is more than what it cuts. The question is not to ask what one can do with a sword but what a sword can do to one who holds it – to the bearers. And to the groups. To the people who associate themselves with the sword. It functions as a symbolic power that has the power to make a group.

Excerpted with permission from Spectacle State: How Hindutva Shapes Feeling and Culture, Brahma Prakash, HarperCollins India.

editorials.title: In Congress-ruled Karnataka, Bengali Muslim migrant workers come under citizenship scrutiny
editorials.passage:
In August last year, Rafikul Biswas was picked up from his home in Bengaluru, and accused of being an undocumented migrant from Bangladesh.

Biswas, who is originally from Nadia district in Bengal, spent four months in a detention centre in the city, as his family members and lawyers scrambled to get him out.

Since May last year, several Bengali Muslims have been picked up in states ruled by the Bharatiya Janata Party, falsely accused of being Bangladeshis and, in several cases, forcibly expelled from Indian territory.

In Biswas’s case, it was the Congress-ruled government in Karnataka that had acted in a similar fashion.

It took a year-long legal battle for Biswas to be set free, despite the fact that he owned a passport. In the time he spent in the detention centre, he suffered two cardiac episodes, Biswas told Scroll .

On August 4, the Karnataka High Court declared the 32-year-old an Indian and said that his family had been residing in India for “generations”.

But his ordeal was not yet over.

Four days later, on August 8, the police landed up at Biswas’s home again at 6 in the morning and rounded him up along with his wife.

They were among about 3,000 Bengali workers picked up by the Bengaluru City Police as part of a special drive, called ‘Operation Mukta’, to identify suspected undocumented immigrants living in the city.

The police raided 90 locations, many of which are home to Bengali speakers who pick up and segregate the tonnes of garbage and waste that Bengaluru produces every day.

“Everyone was picked up and accused of being Bangladeshi,” Biswas said. “In my locality, about 230 people were taken to the police station despite being Indian citizens.” Biswas said the police refused to even see the High Court order declaring him an Indian.

Sheikh Kader, a 56-year-old of Nadia district of Bengal, who has been living in Bengaluru for the last 21 years, said he was picked up from a road near his home by a group of policemen on the morning of August 8.

“I have a long beard and I wear a lungi,” he told Scroll . “They looked at me and said, ‘Aap pura Bangladeshi hai.’” You are definitely a Bangladeshi.

Kader added: “The police did not check any documents before detaining me.”

Hundreds of workers were held for 12-14 hours in detention centres, marriage halls and hotels and then finally let go. Of the 3,000 picked up, only 105 were found to be undocumented migrants from Bangladesh, The Times of India reported .

The mass detention has been criticised by activists as unprecedented for Karnataka.

Hundreds of Indian citizens were harassed in the drive, Avisikta (June), a Bengaluru-based human rights activist who works with displaced and migrant populations, told Scroll .

“There is anyway widespread ethno-racial hate speech in Karnataka against Bengali workers,” Avisikta said. “Every Bengali-speaking informal worker is suspected of being Bangladeshi. This right-wing rhetoric appears to have pushed the Congress to crack down instead of following constitutional provisions.”

Biswas, who has been living in Bengaluru for over 12 years, too, said he was disappointed.

“Sarkar Congress er, kintu byabohaar BJPir,” Biswas said. It is a Congress government here, but it behaves like the BJP.

Scroll emailed and called the Bengaluru police commissioner and the Karnataka home minister Priyank Kharge, asking about the rationale behind the drive and allegations of harassment of Indian citizens. The story will be updated if they reply.

Biswas lives in a shanty in Somasundarpalya with his 30-year-old wife Anguri Khatun Biswas and their 11- year-old daughter. Before he was picked up last year, he was employed as a driver at a private school. He also ran a scrap business.

On the evening of August 28, 2025, personnel from the Bandepalya police station knocked at his door and took him away.

A day later, the Foreigners Regional Registration Office passed an order directing that Biswas be put in a detention centre.

“I was not given any notice nor was I initially told the reason for my confinement,” Biswas told Scroll .

Later, the police showed him purported Bangladeshi identity documents that proved he was a citizen of that country, Biswas said.

His family and friends went to the police with a folder of documents – Biswas’s passport, his school certificate, a voter identity card and an electoral roll featuring his name, his Aadhar card, and a gram panchayat certificate.

Biswas and his wife Anguri Khatun Biswas said they refused to check the papers. “We were told these are fake documents,” Anguri Khatun said.

Two days later, the police in Biswas’s native district, Nadia, carried out an enquiry and submitted a report to the FRRO, confirming that Biswas is an Indian citizen and a permanent resident of Dhananjoypur village. However, he was not released.

The FRRO maintained that he was detained on the basis of information from intelligence agencies as well as documentary evidence – a national ID card from Bangladesh as well as a birth certificate issued by the country.

Biswas’s advocate Clifton D Rozario argued that the two alleged Bangladeshi documents were fake and that the FRRO had issued an order without following due process. “The authorities made no efforts to verify the veracity of these documents,” he said. “A person's citizenship cannot be challenged in such a cavalier fashion.”

Eventually, Biswas’s wife challenged the detention order by FRRO in the Karnataka High Court.

On August 4, the High Court of Karnataka declared him Indian, saying that the voter card issued to him after the recent Special Intensive Revision in West Bengal was “genuine” and that his family had been residing in India for “generations”.

“The Karnataka High court declared me Indian,” Biswas said. “But where is the justice? Where did the police get these two fake Bangladeshi documents to frame me? I need an answer.”

Several Bengali workers, who were raided and detained in this year’s drive, also questioned the police action against them.

Abul Kalam Azad, a 42-year-old resident of Murshidabad who came to the city three months ago for his niece’s treatment, said he was detained for close to a day.

“There was no FIR against me or any complaint. But I had to go to the FRRO the next day and give my biometrics because they suspected I am Bangladeshi,” he said.

Azad said that he never expected a Congress government would doubt his citizenship. “This is not done,” he said.

Aijual Sheikh, a 47-year-old scrap dealer in Electronic City, said several of his workers, who segregate garbage, were accosted and beaten up in a raid on August 8.

“The police can check our documents,” Sheikh said. “But they can’t treat us like thieves and criminals. We are Indians, not Bangladeshis.”

Activists in Bengaluru pointed out that the situation is complicated by the presence of undocumented Bangladeshi migrants in the city, many of whom also work in the waste segregation sector.

“They are often employed at lesser wages than workers from West Bengal and Assam and exploited,” said R Kaleem Ullah, a member of the All India Shramik Swaraj Kendra who has been working with Bengali Muslims in the city for decades.

Activists alleged that the presence of Bangladeshis is not hidden from the police or political parties.

“The police are fully aware of which is a Bangladeshi settlement and which is inhabited by Indian Bengali workers,” said Kaleem Ullah.

The Congress government, he said, was forced to launch the drive against illegal migrants because of pressure from right-wing activists in Bengaluru. In the run-up to the police action, several Hindutva activists had gone around confronting and interrogating migrant workers, accusing them of being undocumented Bangladeshi immigrants, and posted videos .

“The Congress came under pressure and now poor migrant workers are getting harassed,” Kaleem Ullah said.

Indian Bengali Muslims, Avisikta said, have ended up becoming “collateral damage”.

The citizenship trial has set back Rafikul Biswas by many years, he said.

He lost his job as a school driver. His scrap godown and the shanty he was living in were attacked and set on fire in April. He had to take a loan from a moneylender in Bengal to pay his daughter’s school fees.

He alleged that he was kept in solitary confinement at the detention centre, which affected his health. “I did not see the sun for months. Each hour felt like a year.”

Biswas said he was perturbed that his nationality was questioned by the Congress government because he is a Bengali Muslim. “If I get an opportunity, I will question Rahul Gandhi. What is the difference between you and the BJP?”

editorials.title: Two days after Bhagwat’s speech in New York, 90 US politicians pledge to not take RSS-linked funding
editorials.passage:
As Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh Mohan Bhagwat took the stage at New York City’s Madison Square Garden on Saturday to deliver a message of “universal oneness”, a group of nearly 90 American politicians was preparing a different memo: they would not accept political contributions from entities linked to the Hindutva organisation he leads.

The pledge, announced Monday by Hindus for Human Rights Action and SACRED Acts , commits elected officials and candidates across eight American states to reject contributions connected to the RSS and its affiliates. The signatories include members of Congress, state legislators, mayors, local elected officials and candidates from both Democratic and Republican circles.

The six-page pledge also asks politicians to reject political violence and intimidation; and return money from RSS entities and supporters or redirect it to organisations supporting democracy.

Among the most prominent signatories are members of the US House of Representatives Pramila Jayapal of Washington, Ro Khanna of California and Robin Kelly of Illinois. Michigan’s newly-elected Democratic nominee for the Senate race Abdul El-Sayed was among those who signed on, as was New York’s Brad Lander, a Democratic congressional nominee who also attended protests against Bhagwat’s talk in the city on Saturday.

“I’m proud to lead on this pledge and re-assert my commitment to overcome the RSS and their attacks on global democracy,” Khanna said.

For some politicians, the pledge was accompanied by an immediate financial action.

At the forefront of this was Khanna, who said he was returning a $6,600 contribution he recently received “from a pro-MAGA, billionaire with ties to the RSS”.

Khanna said he would not allow the RSS to “create a PAC or influence elections in the US”, he said. In the US, a PAC or political action committee is a private group that pools money from members, donors or employees to fund political campaigns.

Since he was elected to Congress in 2016, Khanna has had close ties with the Hindu-American community and its advocacy groups.

Early in his political career, for example, he attended gatherings organised by the Hindu American Foundation .

The Hindu American Foundation has opposed efforts to explicitly recognise caste discrimination in US law. However, it describes itself as a nonpartisan Hindu civil-rights organisation and has denied any affiliation with the RSS.

Khanna has also received significant campaign contributions from Hindu-American donors who have supported Hindutva causes.

In 2023, The Nation reported that Khanna – who pushed for Prime Minister Narendra Modi to speak at the American Congress that year – received over $110,000 from Hindutva supporters in the US over the preceding 12 years.

In response to these findings, Khanna said that he had thousands of South Asian donors and did not ask each of them about their views on Indian politics.

The same year, Khanna took a more cautious position on an issue that had become a major fault line between Hindutva organisations and anti-caste activists: California’s Senate Bill 403 .

It would have added caste as an explicitly protected category in California’s civil-rights laws. Dalit and anti-caste advocates argued that existing categories did not adequately address caste discrimination and that naming caste explicitly was necessary to make such discrimination visible and enforceable.

Hindu-American organisations, including the Hindu American Foundation, opposed the bill, calling it “discriminatory” and “unconstitutional”.

Khanna did not endorse the bill.

When asked about it in 2023, he said he “strongly opposes any form of caste discrimination” but that legislation needed to be “fairly enforced” so that it did not “selectively profile any community”.

The bill ultimately passed the California state legislature but was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom in October 2023, who said existing protections already prohibited caste discrimination.

Days before Bhagwat’s appearance, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom urged the Trump administration to consider sanctions against RSS members and to bar RSS leaders from entering the United States. The commission’s recommendation was non-binding.

Now, the campaign against RSS influence is moving into another arena: American campaign finance.

SACRED Acts, a collective working to expose “extremist South Asian American groups” in the US, launched its Nonviolence Pledge in Illinois in 2023 with the support of the Indian American Muslim Council, Asian American Midwest Progressives, India Civil Watch International and Hindus for Human Rights. Since then, nearly 90 officials and candidates have signed up across federal, state and local races.

“Over the past decade, in Illinois alone, individuals tied to the RSS have funnelled at least $2.5 million into political campaigns across both parties [Democratic and Republican] promoting their anti-democratic, extremist agenda that does not represent the beliefs of the vast majority of South Asian Americans,” said Pushkar Sharma, the Executive Director of SACRED Acts, in the letter.

The pledge’s organisers say the issue is not confined to whether individual politicians formally accept money from the RSS itself. Their commitment extends to affiliates and individuals they identify as connected to the organisation.

However, tracking how such funds move through American political and social circles is difficult.

Political donations in the United States can move through political action committees, individual donors, affiliated organisations and other entities. In other words, funds connected to the RSS cannot simply be identified by searching a politician’s campaign-finance records for the organisation’s name.

“For far too long, RSS-affiliated organisations and individuals have represented themselves as the only advocates for Hindu Americans in US politics,” said Ria Chakraborty, the Executive Director of Hindus for Human Rights Action. “This pledge and its adoption by almost 100 political leaders is a historic rebuke to the RSS’s misrepresentation of South Asian and Hindu American communities.”

On the same day as this pledge was released, and as Bhagwat headed to the next destination of his trip, Canada, a group in that country announced actions to investigate RSS-related funding.

Just Peace Advocates , a Canadian human rights organisation, said they have filed a complaint with the Canada Revenue Agency asking it to examine the charitable status of 21 registered Canadian charities. They include the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh Canada, Ekal Vidyalaya Foundation of Canada, Vishwa Hindu Parishad of Ontario.

The announcement cites a study by Sciences Po’s Center for International Research that claimed that about $46 million moved between RSS-affiliated organisations in Canada, and $21.5 million was sent from Hindutva organisations to RSS-linked groups abroad.

editorials.title: This book on news photography in India examines how some images became the nation’s visual memory
editorials.passage:
When the Covid pandemic hit around March 2020, death itself lost its meaning because everyone was dying or was on the waiting list to hell. The wail of the ambulance, too, had lost its meaning because that sound had become the only noise in that deadly silence that had descended on the world. In Delhi, there was no space to bury the mounting dead. There was no farewell unless you treated the honking of the ambulance as a dirge or the drumbeats that herald Yama, the god of death. Bodies were being dumped all over. For a news photographer, it could be heaven or hell. How do you capture the inevitability of people dying in front of you? Hospitals were no longer a place to go to recover and live. You went there to die. The transition was uncomplainingly smooth. There were no goodbyes. You were bundled in half-alive and stretched out fully dead. The next stop was the pavement outside the overflowing crematoriums.

About a year into the pandemic, it became evident throughout north India, at least Delhi and Uttar Pradesh, that bodies were being burnt on roadsides and riverbanks. Any empty stretch of open land was turned into a place to dump bodies to be burnt as soon as possible. There was no time to pray for salvation of the soul. No slokas disturbed the fear of those rotten evenings. For photographers trying to show us the scale of devastation and the unfailing routine of death, it was an equally ugly and dangerous endeavour due to greater exposure to the virus. Into this endeavour they had to bring the aesthete’s sense of horrid beauty. How does one make death beautiful and haunting? Can the burning of the dead be immortalised? Will they become posters like that of dead Che? The most haunting picture of the wrath of the pandemic came from Uttar Pradesh. In Ghaziabad, bordering Delhi, Pulitzer Prize-winning Reuters photographer Danish Siddiqui, who was in the prime of his career and had taken some of the most startling photographs in South Asia, flew his drone into an open space that had become a crematorium. The screen of the drone lit up with the many fires of damnation and hell or was it the fires of redemption? Seeing that picture, the world stopped as if it hadn’t already. For the first time, we knew what the end of the earth would be like

Though my former colleague Qamar Sibtain also shot the burning pyres, he also shot a rather haunting picture inside the Parliament building of a Congress leader, Digvijay Singh, all dressed up in a protective suit, climbing down the stairs alone after voting in a Rajya Sabha election, looking as if he is descending to the unknown. There is no one else in the frame, just the stone walls of the building giving it a haunting feel. While all the pictures showed us the horror and the scale of the pandemic, PTI’s photographer Atul Yadav captured the most heart-rending picture, showing how broken the people were, with neither hope for the living nor salvation for the dead. Yadav was going along the Nizamuddin bridge in East Delhi to shoot pictures of the mass reverse migration of labourers left to fend for themselves. On the bridge, he saw a man seated on the pavement, with his mask half pulled out and crying on the phone.

“That some images may have the shock factor for some viewers is completely their perspective. It's not my intention. Perhaps pictures that have an emotional factor, pictures that touch our hearts, are much more powerful and remembered,” Arko Datta, who shot the iconic picture of a tearful and utterly fearful Ansari pleading in front of the camera during the Gujarat riots of 2002, told me. Arko should know because to him belongs another heart-wrenching picture that has come to symbolise despair and never-ending sorrow and tragic fate that follows India’s poor: the picture of a lady lying on the beach, her hands turned towards heaven in prayer, as her husband’s body washes up, after the tsunami of 2004 in Cuddalore on the Tamil Nadu coast. In its sheer helplessness and deep sorrow, in that final appeal to the gods who left her alone to face the world, that picture will stand out forever. So much power and despair and utter sadness reach out of that frame.

The dead remain with us. That signifies the end of hope and the beginning of a dark age for the woman and maybe for others like Arko’s picture. But men do cry too, though not as heart-wrenching as when a woman cries by the side of her dear dead. Outside the mortuary of Delhi’s Lal Manohar Lohia hospital, two young men collapsed into each other’s arms in total sorrow, just a few drops of tears glistening on one man’s face, after being told of the death of their dear one in the Delhi riots of 2022. To be there at such moments of private sorrow is the photographer’s calling. The man next to them is totally unconcerned, though he too might be nursing his sorrow outside the mortuary. The signboard is a giveaway for sure but that simple, spontaneous act of comforting each other is so numbing.

Excerpted with permission from All in a Flash: News Photography in India, Binoo K John, Niyogi Books.

editorials.title: The higher Asim Munir climbs, the shakier Pakistan gets
editorials.passage:
Recently, social media showed a picture of General Asim Munir posing for a photograph with Harvard Business School students, that too in full uniform, along with his No.1 public relations man, Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry. Harvard can hardly be given a black mark for this visit. After all, Munir is being feted by one and all, including the mercurial US President. All this, however, matters hugely for Munir. It seems to set the seal on his rise, and his general acceptability as a virtual king of all he surveys. But there are strong upheavals below the surface. And it’s not just that almost the whole of Pakistan is in protest mode. There’s worse.

The Iran relationship is difficult
First, even as Munir is being toasted as the ‘mediator extraordinaire’, the reality is that relations with Iran are not looking good on the ground. Tehran hasn’t backed off from pursuing arbitration in France on the stalled Iran-Pakistan pipeline (IPP), originally supposed to have been completed in 2015, with repeated failures to import the agreed-upon 750 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd) of gas triggering the arbitration process after Pakistan missed a September 2024 deadline. Initially signed in 2009, Pakistan says the delays are due to US sanctions. That is true only in part. Pakistan has never been known to keep to its project deadlines, including with regard to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, or the Reko Diq mine, where it only just managed to avoid a hefty penalty by the Arbitration Court of $5.84 billion in damages in 2011. Now Iran may get over $18 billion in arbitration fees.

Then there’s the trade issue. With Trump announcing ‘Operation Economic Fury’, which will impose secondary sanctions on all countries trading with Iran, there’s trouble ahead, or should be. Pakistan’s Ministry of Commerce in April had announced six new routes into Iran through the ‘Transit of Goods through Territory of Pakistan Order 2026’. The order allows goods originating from third countries to be transported through Pakistan and delivered to Iran by road. As data shows, Gwadar has suddenly emerged as a port of choice, after remaining in limbo for a decade. Karachi says it’s making more money in a single day than it made in the last decade. This, together with Pakistan’s own estimated $1.3 billion in imports from Iran, would be in jeopardy if Trump is serious.

Indeed, Pakistan’s foreign ministry issued a carefully worded statement citing Pakistan’s adherence to international law, and noting, rather mysteriously, that ‘as such, our trade remains in consonance with our obligations’. That says nothing. In the event, the US sanctioned one obscure firm, Allianz Energy — already under sanctions — and four Indian firms for trading in sums that are as low as $25 million. That says much, given that both trade at the same volume in bilateral terms. In sum, the sanctions completely ignored the ‘transit’ aspect. Gen Munir was in Tehran that very day, and clearly still in the mediating business. One-all for Pakistan, but the ground is perilous. Meanwhile, sources like Al Jazeera don’t even mention Pakistan as a major source of Iranian trade, transit or otherwise. That’s good media management. India, of course, gets ‘top customer’ billing.

The IMF takes a dim view
Less give was apparent in the recent refusal by the International Monetary Fund to loosen controls on Pakistan. The IMF is trying to curtail the powers of the Federal Government to make a downward revision in gas prices, in an effort to prevent further accumulation of circular debt, which has ballooned to some PKR 4.9 trillion. That’s a lot, and there’s no getting around it. Worse, Moody’s has tried hard to be a little more imaginative in presenting a positive picture of Pakistan, noting that it is ‘marginally less likely to default than before’.

Meanwhile, it noted a narrow export base, negligible FDI, reliance on remittances and borrowing, and governance failures, including weak rule of law, poor control of corruption and limited government effectiveness. The Dawn editorial gloomily notes that ‘standing still while the rest of the world advances is nothing but a quiet form of decline’. And arising from that, Pakistan will do nothing to stop the smuggling of oil from Iran, worth some $1 billion in 2024. That amount would have multiplied by at least ten, given that it is also coming by sea, accounting for some 14 per cent of Pakistan’s oil consumption.

Islamabad is not going to risk ending that. Neither are its border forces. In 2016, 12 officers, including a Lieutenant General of the Frontier Corps, most posted together in Balochistan, were sacked for corruption. That preceded Nawaz Sharif’s ousting on corruption charges as well, and was intended to send a message of ‘accountability’ across the board. No other generals or even lower-level officers have since faced scrutiny. But it’s one of those open secrets that abound. The army is making money hand over fist.

The police are fed up
While the army enjoys its perks, which include posh bungalows and SUVs — not to mention the inevitable gifting of prime land at retirement — the police are rebelling. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police have long been complaining that the presence of the army is making them more vulnerable, not less, to terrorist attacks. A protest erupted in the districts of Bannu and Lakki Marwat by members of the Police Aman Committee. Those protests began after the disappearance of a member of the Lakki Marwat peace committee. The rage was apparent as police forced banks to close, and were joined even by traffic police.

This was the second time such protests had taken place. Earlier, on August 25, committee members protested against the transfer of seven Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa police officials to other districts and demanded that the orders be withdrawn. Given the chaos, the Inspector General of Police (IGP) had to request that nine platoons of the Federal Constabulary (FC) be deployed for ‘protection of vital installations’.
The letter also noted ‘extreme’ difficulties in the movement of officers of the district administration, judiciary and other government officials, and ‘explicit threats’ to officers, among other serious issues. It may be recalled that police units have got short shrift when terrorists strike. Bannu in particular has been the target of terrorist strikes, with more than 20 policemen dying in attacks in May.

The key aspect was that in this and other strikes, army reinforcements failed to arrive, leading to accusations that the military is holed up in its cantonments. Such total police opposition is not new, with police in Kurram and nearby agencies refusing to work with the army, and accusing it — rather significantly — of sheltering terrorists. But now it seems that, like all other protests, the situation is escalating.

The Imran Khan question
The issue of the jailed former Prime Minister, Imran Khan, is essentially Asim Munir’s Achilles’ heel. Dead, he could start a riot. Alive and free, he could become a nuisance. But the point is, meanwhile, the arrests of leaders of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf continue.

Recently, an anti-terrorism court (ATC) in Rawalpindi sentenced 47 PTI leaders and workers to ten years’ imprisonment each for their alleged involvement in the May 9, 2023 attack on General Headquarters. The court also ordered the confiscation of their properties and imposed a fine of Rs 500,000. This list includes senior PTI figures such as Omar Ayub, Zartaj Gul, Murad Saeed, Shibli Faraz, Hammad Azhar and Shahbaz Gill, though none of them turned up. Inside jail, no one has any idea of the exact number of PTI party members jailed, with a record 108 jailed last year, apart from leading figures such as Dr Yasmin Rashid and Shah Mahmood Qureshi.

During National Assembly elections in 2024, PTI members running as independent candidates won the most seats, but were blocked from forming a government. All this is likely to breed huge resentment, and any single event could lead to an overspill. Apparently, however, the present policy of jailing every major leader and smaller ones has ‘delivered’ so far.

There is heartburn in the army
And at the end of the list, and probably the most dangerous of all for the life and times of Munir, was Lt Gen Aamer Raza’s promotion to four-star rank in July 2026 to head the newly created National Strategic Command. Pakistani media reported him as only eighth in the lieutenant-general seniority hierarchy and promoted over Inam Haider Malik, Fayyaz Hussain Shah, Nauman Zakaria, Muhammad Zafar Iqbal, Ahsan Gulrez and Shahid Imtiaz. Lt Gen Asim Malik, the most senior, remained in place on an extended tenure as ISI chief.

Military Secretary Lt Gen Shahid Imtiaz, also from the 22nd cohort of OTS (Officers Training School) and now in the powerful post of Military Secretary, may well continue. But for the others, it’s probably retirement time. This process gets worse if Munir continues beyond November 2027 as COAS, which seems highly likely. The only course left open to the ambitious Munir is to create more posts for the upwardly mobile. That will probably mean virtual martial law.

As General Munir trips lightly from country to country, and is greeted by the world’s most powerful leaders, he would be hard put to forget that landing back home is a tricky issue each time. From the ‘crate of mangoes’ that decimated General Zia-ul-Haq and an entire slab of senior officers, to the aircraft carrying General Musharraf that was nearly prevented from landing in Pakistan, it’s a tricky business. But even having landed safely, his troubles are only likely to multiply, with more and more problems coming up as a sullen country deals with a near collapse of governance and the inequities heaped on it.

The problem for India remains the same. The more Munir goes down, the more risk he will be willing to take to provoke India to war. Remember, it was after Operation Sindoor that he took the first step on that ladder of ambition. He’s not done yet.

(The writer is a former Director, National Security Council Secretariat. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Head-on | Why Pakistan’s Mecca shield won’t blunt India’s sword
editorials.passage:
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan lends itself to several interpretations. The text of the agreement, signed on August 7, 2026, in Mecca, has still not been released. A joint statement and press release are light on details of the pact, perhaps deliberately.

The meeting in Istanbul on August 31 between the defence and foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, along with their military chiefs, was long on rhetoric but short on substance. The prospect of Egypt and Bangladesh joining the Mecca Agreement could make it as unwieldy as the equally toothless Pakistan-Kuwait defence protocol signed in Rawalpindi on August 27.

What are the Mecca Agreement’s principal objectives? In a word, deterrence.

Since none of the three signatories — Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan — are direct participants in the ongoing US-Israel-Iran war, the Mecca Agreement has a narrow agenda.

The first is to deter retaliatory Iranian and Houthi attacks on Saudi oil refineries and ships. That objective came undone within 48 hours of the agreement being signed when the Houthis fired projectiles at the Aramco oil refinery in Jazan, a city in southwestern Saudi Arabia.

Did Turkey or Pakistan rush to Saudi Arabia’s defence? Clearly not.

The second interpretation of the Mecca Agreement is that it reduces America’s military commitment in West Asia. US President Donald Trump has long said that regional powers should take care of regional problems.

In Europe, he has told America’s NATO partners to increase their defence budgets from 2 per cent to 5 per cent of GDP in order to defend themselves from Russia and not depend on American military help.

Is the same message going out in West Asia? Last year’s Saudi-Pakistan defence pact was endorsed by Trump. The Mecca pact, which adds Turkey, has also been endorsed by Washington. Will it reduce US military involvement in West Asia? No. The problems for the US in the Gulf are Iran and Israel. One is its mortal enemy, the other its closest ally.

America has 19 military bases in the Gulf with a deployment of nearly 50,000 US military personnel directly under US Central Command (CENTCOM). They will stay there till the Iran conflict is resolved. Trump ordered the aircraft carrier USS George Washington to relocate from South Korea to West Asia. Not one of America’s 11 aircraft carriers remains in the Indo-Pacific. That is a clear sign of intent: West Asia is central to Washington’s geopolitical strategy.

In India, the Mecca Agreement has evoked concern, most of it unjustified. The concern revolves around a future India-Pakistan war: will Turkey and Saudi Arabia come to Islamabad’s aid in such an event?

They won’t because the Mecca Agreement is a defence pact, as its official title suggests. During Operation Sindoor, Turkish weaponry was widely — and unsuccessfully — used by Pakistan from its stored inventory. Saudi Arabia maintained silent neutrality.

Saudi Arabia can barely defend itself against Iranian and Houthi missile and drone attacks. It commissioned Pakistan’s former army chief Raheel Sharif as far back as 2015 to take command of an Islamic force, led by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), to fight in the Yemen civil war. Eleven years later, the civil war remains unresolved. The rebel Yemen-based Houthis remain a potent force. The breakdown in relations between Saudi Arabia and the UAE over the Yemen war has caused a rift between the Gulf’s two wealthiest countries. Both have strong economic relations with India.

If the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement is an impotent pact, why is Pakistan treating it as an added arrow in its quiver aimed at India? After suffering a devastating defeat in the four-day war against India during Operation Sindoor, following the terrorist attack in Pahalgam that killed 25 Indian tourists and one local guide, Pakistan has been on a diplomatic overdrive.

Army Chief Asim Munir has positioned himself as a peacemaker in the US-Iran war, flattered Trump by proposing him for the Nobel Peace Prize, and signed lucrative crypto deals with Trump’s two sons, Eric and Don Jr.

Islamabad is meanwhile beset with internal strife: Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) is in violent revolt; the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) is striking military targets across the country at will; both Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK) are in ferment. The continuing incarceration of former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan, defying a Supreme Court order to shift him to Shifa International Hospital, has alienated the country’s influential middle class.

For Munir and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif — who has surrendered power to Munir — the Mecca Agreement is a useful device. It places Pakistan at the heart of West Asia as a security guarantor and the only Muslim country with nuclear weapons.

The underlying contest in West Asia is between a Sunni alliance led by Saudi Arabia and Turkey and an arc of Shia nations led by Iran, curving from Lebanon in the west to Yemen in the east. Pakistan is the odd man out. It is Sunni-majority but is neither Arab nor has Turkey’s Ottoman lineage.

More than 9.6 million Indians live and work in West Asia. Nearly 3.9 million are based in the UAE and 2.7 million in Saudi Arabia. The rest are scattered across the GCC region, principally in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and Oman.

How will the Mecca Agreement impact them? Not in the slightest. What will impact them — and already has — is the US-Israel-Iran war. Since Israel and the US launched their attack on Iran on February 28, 2026, several Indian ships have been attacked in the crossfire in the Strait of Hormuz. Dozens of Indian seafarers have lost their lives.

Despite the conflict, however, remittances from the Gulf have held firm. In the April-June 2026 quarter, at the height of the Iran war, remittances rose significantly. They now account for 38-40 per cent of $145 billion in annual global remittances from Indians abroad. A large part of the nearly $100 billion raised in RBI’s FCNR scheme has come from the Gulf.

At the end of the day, the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement is unlikely to ever be operationalised in any theatre of conflict. That is perhaps why the text of the agreement remains sealed, immune to public scrutiny.

(The writer is an editor, author and publisher. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Is Mohan Bhagwat's Lament Against ‘Me, Myself’ Politics a Message for Modi?
editorials.passage: Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat recently expressed his frustration with politics, with an unequivocal condemnation of the “me, myself” malaise. For him, politics hasn’t lived up to expectations to bring desired changes in the society. Bhagwat, in his comments in Madison Square Garden, New York, further blamed politics for the prevalence of “self-interest”. On the surface, Bhagwat’s comments may seem general in nature, but the possibility that he was signalling to Prime Minister Narendra Modi cannot be ruled out.Did Bhagwat send a subtle message to Modi? The answer is most likely yes, because Modi has exercised an almost absolute dominance over Indian politics for the past 12 years. Yet the RSS chief sounded dissatisfied.“…change is not happening through politics alone. I am sorry to say, but politics has largely become a game of self-interest,” Bhagwat remarked, as he spoke at the MSG, New York during the ‘One World, One Humanity’ conference. The RSS chief further qualified his comments, saying that “… wherever there is ‘me’ and ‘mine’, there is no solution, ‘we’ and ‘ours’ is the only solution.”One could argue that the RSS chief was referring to world leaders in the context of unresolved global conflicts. But it may be emphasised that Bhagwat underlined the inadequacies of politics in bringing about changes while highlighting interventions that “we’ve already begun" directly through “society”.Favouring the “we, ours” approach as a way to achieve solutions, Bhagwat appeared to make his preference clear for collective leadership.Mysterious New Outfit Hosting Mohan Bhagwat in New York Has Old RSS LinksSince 2024, the RSS Chief has made several remarks, which have been seen as being directed at the Prime Minister. Bhagwat, true to form, rarely makes direct comments about political personalities but rather speaks through innuendos and indirect references.Bhagwat’s remarks made in Ranchi in 2024, that “one shouldn’t claim himself to be a God,” had also been widely interpreted as reflecting his displeasure with Modi’s cultivation of a personality cult within Indian politics. In another comment, Bhagwat had raised the issue of the unabated violence in Manipur, stating “the state is still awaiting peace.” The RSS chief also has, in the past, sounded displeased with electioneering turning into personal sparring. After the 2024 elections, Bhagwat had said that “decorum wasn’t maintained in elections.”Besides Bhagwat’s past remarks, the RSS-BJP relations remain fluid. As Modi approaches the age of 76 on 17 September and the BJP commemorates a fortnight of the “service outreach” to commemorate the PM's birthday, the spotlight keeps returning on the “who after Modi?” question. Last year, in the weeks preceding Modi’s 75th birthday, feverish speculations ran through India’s political capital about the future of Modi’s tenure as Prime Minister. That question is resurfacing again.100 Years of RSS Has Also Seen 100 Years of ResistanceAlso, Bhagwat within the RSS-BJP ideological family, is arguably the only person who will be the final arbiter of the leadership transition in the saffron political outfit. In 2013 also, Bhagwat is widely believed to have brought peace to the BJP by persuading LK Advani and Sushma Swaraj to back Modi as the party's PM face for the 2014 Lok Sabha elections. That explains the exalted position of the RSS chief in relation to the BJP, which cannot risk snapping the ties and asserting full autonomy as a major chunk of the cadres of both the outfits comes from a common pool.Modi’s style of functioning, marked by excessive centralisation of power and decision-making, has been his hallmark. In Gujarat, as the Chief Minister of the state, Modi's office became almost the sole decision-making centre. Old timers recall that bureaucrats were more powerful than ministers in Modi’s Gujarat days. But he was still a Gujarat leader, and the BJP at the national stage, boasted of a number of influential leaders who together gave a sense of collective leadership within the party.As in Gujarat, where he had gradually and slowly consolidated his authority with influential leaders either leaving the BJP or getting marginalised, Modi replicated his Gujarat model with full force after winning the massive mandate in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections. After that, the BJP seemed transformed as an electioneering extension of 'brand Modi'. The BJP’s fortnight-long service outreach, called “Seva Sankalp Abhiyan”, starting on the PM's birthday, is an unmistakable example of the outfit amplifying the personal image of Modi.Mohan Bhagwat's Vijayadashami Speech Marks a ‘Global’ Shift in the RSS PlaybookBhagwat spoke of influencing policies in his MSG remarks in New York. That suggests that the RSS has a wish list on the policy front. The RSS regularly holds “Samanway Baithak”, or coordination meetings, in which all its affiliates take part, including the BJP. This meeting is actually seen as the forum through which the RSS and its other affiliates communicate their priorities to the BJP, which in turn conveys the message to the government.The RSS, per insiders, is growing alarmed that the excessive centralisation of leadership is now showing visible signs of governance gaps, as well as creating a political void within the BJP. While it may be said that the youth has seen past the façade of shining 'brand Modi' in the course of their three-week-long protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, the RSS' concerns did not emerge after the protests alone.The RSS has indeed been counting the episodes — the Modi government couldn’t deliver on the National Education Policy 2020, a key interest area of the Nagpur-headquartered outfit; the social rupture after the contentious UGC resolution; the furore over the Aravalli rule (stayed by the Supreme Court); Modi’s US foreign policy, which has alarmed the RSS and its affiliates on economic issues; and, worryingly for the RSS, the deepening of the caste divide.Lately, the RSS has been dropping hints of eagerness to not be seen as being clubbed with the BJP. To this effect, the RSS has intensified its own outreach. The RSS leaders have been discussing the risks of being seen through the BJP prism as the Modi-centric governance model and politics of the BJP begin to reveal cracks.(Author is a senior Delhi-based journalist, who for over two decades has reported on the BJP, the RSS, and the PMO. This is an opinion piece and the views expressed above are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for the same.)

editorials.title: Modi’s Peace Pitch to Putin Has One Big Problem—India’s Own Foreign Policy
editorials.passage: Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit for their first meeting of the year.What stood out in the meeting was Modi’s admonition to Putin that “we must move from ‘endless war’ to ‘end of war’ for the benefit of humanity,” in an explicit reference to the Ukraine conflict. This was an echo of his 2022 message at the Samarkand SCO summit, where he told the Russian leader that “now is not an era of war.” At the time, the remark was widely praised and cited across global diplomatic circles. This time around, however, the fact that Modi read the statement off a slip of paper in his hand robbed the moment of its spontaneous gravitas.In his broader remarks, the Prime Minister invoked “the path to peace” as the foundational message from the land of Gandhi and Buddha, noting that “every day spent in war sets humanity back, whereas every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm.” It was a statement clearly tailored to garner headlines back home—and, predictably, main national daily newspapers led with it the following morning. Yet, just as Putin paid little heed to the message in 2022, he is unlikely to act on it now.Xi-Putin Bonhomie Puts India's BRICS and Quad Bets Under StrainQuestions also remain over how seriously Moscow or the wider international community can take moral exhortations from a leader who maintains a muted posture on other major conflicts, such as the American-Israeli confrontation with Iran. On that front, New Delhi has confined its posture strictly to routine calls for restraint, dialogue, and diplomacy.Even on the day he met Putin, Modi also held bilateral talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. In a post on X, Modi framed the exchange in broad terms, noting simply that they discussed ongoing conflicts and that “India will continue to support all efforts aimed at ensuring lasting peace.” The official readout of the talks noted that the PM “reiterated India’s consistent positions that all issues must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.” And in an oblique dig at Iran, also called for safeguarding the freedom of navigation and commerce. Beyond the issue of war and peace, Putin and Modi also took up bilateral cooperation across a range of vital sectors. Of primary interest to all is energy security, specifically oil trade. Last month in August, India imported between 2.1 and 2.6 million barrels per day, with Russia remaining India’s largest supplier, accounting for roughly 40 percent of total crude imports.In a striking development, India has even exported refined gasoline back to Russia to offset domestic refining disruptions caused by Ukrainian strikes.In their discussions, Modi and Putin would have almost certainly discussed the looming threat of US secondary sanctions—specifically proposed 100 percent tariffs on nations continuing robust trade with Russia and Iran—as Washington pushes New Delhi to diversify toward American and Venezuelan crude.Defense procurement remains another critical friction point. Despite supply-chain disruptions stemming from the Ukraine conflict, Moscow has offered India five additional units of the S-400 long-range surface-to-air missile system, which proved pivotal during Operation Sindoor last year.As for Iran, oil trade which was once flourishing is now dead, strangled by the American secondary sanctions. Iran is the closest source of hydrocarbons to India, yet New Delhi has had to forgo imports because of American policy. Again, India had a flourishing export trade in agricultural products like tea and rice, and pharmaceuticals, which has now been disrupted by war and will now be further affected as UAE, which functioned as a transhipment hub has blocked trade with Iran. Bilateral trade has fallen more than 90 percent since 2018-19 on account of US pressure.Caught between US, Iran, and Russia, Can India Keep its Commitment to BRICS?Ultimately, it is difficult to overlook the transaction-driven cynicism undergirding New Delhi’s approach to both Moscow and Tehran. Pressed against the wall, Iranian leadership had little choice but to publicly appreciate “New Delhi’s support and cooperation with the Islamic Republic of Iran during the recent war.” In a comprehensive three-page statement following the Modi-Pezeshkian , the Iranian leadership quoted Modi directly, noting that even through this difficult period, both sides “sought to maintain and preserve our cooperation and communications.” In another telling excerpt from the Iranian statement, Modi reportedly agreed that there were “groups that see their interests in the continuation of war,” while adding that in his view, “ultimately peace and security will prevail.”This combination—a stand-offish posture toward Tehran alongside public idealism riding on transactionalism toward Moscow—underscores a worldview firmly anchored in staying close to Washington.   India’s grand strategy requires a vigourous balance between continental Eurasian realities and maritime Indo-Pacific commitments. At present, however, that strategy appears dangerously out of alignment: the continental dimension is being sidelined, even as the maritime pillar struggles to stay afloat while Washington steadily undermines the vitality of the Quad.(The writer is a Distinguished Fellow, Observer Research Foundation, New Delhi. This is an opinion piece and the views expressed are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for them.)
